The lessons use tools from probability, linear algebra, analysis, convex optimization, information theory and stochastic calculus. This page recalls each of them from scratch: why the course needs it, the picture to keep in mind, the precise statement, a small example with numbers, a short proof when it helps, the classical mistakes, and where it shows up in machine learning.

How to use this page

You do not need to read it in order. Arrive from a lesson through a link, read the reminder you need, go back. Every reminder (a subsection below) has the same layout:

  • a line “Used in”, saying which lessons need it and for what;
  • the picture to keep in mind, then the precise statement in a box. When a course resource states it, the reference is given: “OT4ML Def. 2.10, p. 23” is the book Optimal Transport for Machine Learners (ressources/OT4ML.pdf), statement number and PDF page. The other facts are standard textbook material and are presented as such;
  • a worked example with small numbers (all of them were checked by computer), a proof or proof sketch (folded: click to open), the pitfalls, and, when there is one, an application in machine learning.

Section 9 summarises the optimal-transport results that every lesson takes for granted, with links to the lessons where they are proved. Lessons 4 to 8 are prepared before the lectures; their links point to the lesson pages as they are written.

1. Probability measures#

A probability measure spreads one unit of mass over a space; you can integrate functions against it, move it with a map, couple it with another one, and say when a sequence of them converges.

Measures, Diracs, densities, integrals#

Used in every lesson: the objects that optimal transport compares (data sets, densities, model distributions) are probability measures. See also the refresher of Lesson 3.

Think of a pile of sand of total mass 1 spread over a space X. A probability measure α tells you how much sand lies in each region: α(A) is the mass in the set A. You can also weigh a function with it: ∫fdα is the average of f when each point counts with its share of sand.

In the course OT4ML Def. 2.1–2.2, p. 20; Def. 2.5, p. 21; Def. 2.6, p. 22; Def. 2.9, p. 23

A probability measure α∈M1+​(X) is a positive measure of total mass α(X)=1. The three kinds used all the time:

  • Dirac δx​: δx​(A)=1 if x∈A, 0 otherwise. Then ∫fdδx​=f(x).
  • Discrete measure α=∑i=1n​ai​δxi​​ with weights in the probability simplex Σn​={a∈R+n​: ∑i​ai​=1} (a histogram). Then α(A)=∑xi​∈A​ai​ and ∫fdα=∑i​ai​f(xi​). The empirical measure of a point cloud is n1​∑i​δxi​​.
  • Density: dα(x)=ρα​(x)dx, so α(A)=∫A​ρα​ and ∫fdα=∫fρα​dx. More generally, if α is absolutely continuous with respect to λ (α≪λ: λ(A)=0⇒α(A)=0), its relative density dλdα​ (Radon–Nikodym derivative) satisfies ∫hdα=∫hdλdα​dλ.

Probabilistic reading: a random variable X has law α (written X∼α) if P(X∈A)=α(A); then E[f(X)]=∫fdα.

supp(α)
The support: the smallest closed set carrying all the mass (for ∑i​ai​δxi​​ with ai​>0: the points xi​).
α⊥β
Mutually singular: they live on disjoint sets (a discrete measure and a density are always mutually singular).
Pp​(Rd)
Measures with a finite p-th moment, ∫∥x∥pdα(x)<∞. This is where Wp​ is finite.
Worked example — a mixed measure

Let α=21​δ0​+21​U[0,2]: half of the mass sits at 0, the other half is spread uniformly on [0,2] (density 21​⋅21​=41​ there).

  • α({0})=21​ (an atom), α({1})=0 (the density part gives no mass to a point), α((0,1])=21​⋅21​=41​, α([0,1])=21​+41​=43​.
  • Mean: ∫xdα=21​⋅0+21​⋅1=21​. Second moment: 21​⋅0+21​⋅34​=32​. Variance: 32​−41​=125​.
Pitfall — a density is not a probability

U[0,21​] has density 2 on [0,21​]: densities can exceed 1; only their integral is 1. The “probability of a point” is 0 for a measure with a density. And δx​ has no density with respect to dx: the “Dirac function” of physics is a measure, not a function.

In machine learning — data sets and models are measures

A data set of n images with d pixels is the empirical measure α^n​=n1​∑i​δxi​​ on Rd; a generative model is a measure αθ​ with a density, or a push-forward of noise (next reminder). Training means making αθ​ close to α^n​, so we need discrepancies that make sense between a discrete measure and a continuous one. The total variation between them is always 2 (Lesson 3) and the KL divergence is +∞ (§6): this is the first argument for transport distances.

Push-forward of a measure, change of variables#

Used in Lesson 1 (Monge’s constraint T#​α=β), Lessons 2–3 (marginals of a plan are push-forwards by the projections; displacement interpolation §6 of Lesson 3), Lesson 5 (projections x↦⟨θ,x⟩), Lesson 6 (flows), and every generative model.

Move each grain of sand from x to T(x): the new pile is the push-forward T#​α. The mass that lands in a set B is the mass that came from the points sent into B.

In the course OT4ML Def. 2.10, p. 23; Remark 2.13, p. 25

For a measurable map T:X→Y and α∈M1+​(X), the push-forward β=T#​α is defined, for every measurable B⊂Y, by

β(B)=α({x∈X: T(x)∈B}),equivalently∫Y​h(y)dβ(y)=∫X​h(T(x))dα(x)

for every bounded measurable h. For a discrete measure, T#​(∑i​ai​δxi​​)=∑i​ai​δT(xi​)​: the weights travel with their points. If X∼α then T(X)∼T#​α.

Push-forward of a density OT4ML Prop. 2.12, p. 24

Let T:U→V be a C1 diffeomorphism between open sets of Rd and α=ρα​dx. Then β=T#​α has a density ρβ​, given by

ρα​(x)=∣detT′(x)∣ρβ​(T(x)),i.e.ρβ​(y)=​detT′(T−1(y))​ρα​(T−1(y))​.

On the line with T increasing: ρβ​(T(x))T′(x)=ρα​(x). Where T compresses (T′<1) the density goes up; where it stretches (T′>1) it goes down.

Worked example — T(x)=x2/2 on U[0,2]
  • By the definition: β([0,y])=α({x: x2/2≤y})=α([0,2y​])=22y​​ for 0≤y≤2; differentiating, ρβ​(y)=22y​1​ on (0,2].
  • By the formula: T−1(y)=2y​ and T′(x)=x, so ρβ​(y)=2y​1/2​. Same result: large near 0 (compression), small near 2 (stretching).
  • Integrating against β without its density: ∫ydβ=∫Tdα=21​E[X2]=21​⋅34​=32​, the same as ∫02​22y​y​dy.
Proof of the density formula

Take a test function h and change variables y=T(x), dy=∣detT′(x)∣dx (§4):

∫h(y)ρβ​(y)dy=∫h(T(x))ρα​(x)dx=∫h(y)​detT′(T−1(y))​ρα​(T−1(y))​dy.

The first equality is the definition of T#​α, the second the change of variables. Two densities with the same integral against every h are equal almost everywhere.

Pitfalls
  • ρβ​=ρα​∘T−1: forgetting the Jacobian factor gives a function that does not integrate to 1.
  • If T is not injective, add the contributions of all the preimages: ρβ​(y)=∑x:T(x)=y​ρα​(x)/∣T′(x)∣ in 1D (Exercise 12 of the Lesson 1 sheet is of this kind).
  • A map cannot split mass: T#​δx​=δT(x)​ is always a single Dirac. This is why no map sends δ0​ to 21​δ−1​+21​δ1​, and why Monge’s problem can have no solution (§9).
In machine learning — generative models are push-forwards

A GAN generator, a VAE decoder, a normalizing flow and a diffusion or flow-matching sampler all define the model as αθ​=(Gθ​)#​ζ, with ζ=N(0,I) and Gθ​ a network: to sample, draw z∼ζ and output Gθ​(z). The density of αθ​ is usually unknown (or does not exist when the latent dimension is smaller than the data dimension), so the training loss must be computable from samples — transport distances and MMD are (OT4ML §7.4, p. 134). Normalizing flows instead keep Gθ​ invertible and use the density formula above (§4).

Joint laws, marginals, independence#

Used in Lesson 2 (transport plans are matrices with prescribed row and column sums), Lesson 3 (general couplings, gluing), Lesson 4 (duality), Lesson 7 (the entropy of a plan measures its dependence).

A joint law describes a pair (X,Y); forgetting one coordinate gives a marginal. In the discrete case it is a table: the marginals are its row sums and its column sums. A coupling of α and β is any table with these row and column sums — any way of pairing the mass of α with the mass of β.

In the course OT4ML Def. 3.25, p. 63; Def. 3.26, Remark 3.27, Def. 3.28, p. 64

For π∈M1+​(X×Y) with projections PX​(x,y)=x, PY​(x,y)=y, the marginals are π1​=(PX​)#​π and π2​=(PY​)#​π. The set of couplings is

U(α,β)={π∈M1+​(X×Y): π1​=α, π2​=β}.

If (X,Y)∼π∈U(α,β) then X∼α and Y∼β; the coupling encodes their dependence. The product α⊗β (independence) is always a coupling; (Id,T)#​α encodes the deterministic relation Y=T(X). Discrete case: U(a,b)={P∈R+n×m​: P1m​=a, P⊤1n​=b}.

Independence. X and Y are independent iff π=α⊗β iff E[f(X)g(Y)]=E[f(X)]E[g(Y)] for all bounded f,g. Independence implies Cov(X,Y)=0, not conversely.

Worked example — all the couplings of two histograms on {0,1}

Take a=(21​,21​) and b=(41​,43​), both on the points {0,1}. The row and column constraints leave one free parameter p=P11​:

P(p)=(p41​−p​21​−p41​+p​),0≤p≤41​.
  • The set of couplings is a segment. Its middle point p=81​=a1​b1​ is the independent coupling (Cov(X,Y)=0); its ends p=0 and p=41​ have covariances −81​ and +81​.
  • With the cost ∣x−y∣, moving mass costs P12​+P21​=43​−2p, smallest at p=41​: cost 41​. Only a quarter of the mass has to move from 0 to 1. (The minimum is at an end of the segment: §5, linear programming.)
Pitfalls
  • The marginals do not determine the joint law: U(α,β) is usually huge (dimension (n−1)(m−1) for histograms).
  • Zero covariance is not independence: X uniform on {−1,0,1} and Y=X2 have Cov(X,Y)=E[X3]−E[X]E[X2]=0, but P(X=0,Y=1)=0=P(X=0)P(Y=1)=92​.
  • A coupling is not a map: a row of P can have several nonzero entries (mass is split).
In machine learning — choosing a coupling between noise and data

Flow matching (Lesson 6) draws pairs (X0​,X1​) from a coupling of the noise N(0,I) and the data, and learns to move X0​ to X1​. With the independent coupling the straight paths cross; with an optimal-transport coupling computed on each minibatch they are shorter and straighter, which makes sampling cheaper (OT4ML Example 16.2 and Fig. 16.1, p. 408). In domain adaptation or single-cell biology the coupling between two unpaired data sets is precisely the unknown matching to infer (OT4ML Examples 3.22 and 3.24, p. 61).

Conditional laws and disintegration#

Used in Lesson 3 (the gluing lemma), Lesson 4 (barycentric projection of a plan), Lesson 6 (the flow-matching velocity is a conditional expectation), Lesson 7 (conditional laws of entropic plans).

Slice the joint law at X=x and renormalise: you get the law of Y given X=x. For a transport plan, it says where the mass located at x is sent.

Definition (standard)
  • Discrete: P(Y=yj​∣X=xi​)=ai​Pij​​ for ai​>0. Densities: ρ(y∣x)=ρ(x,y)/ρX​(x).
  • Disintegration (on Rd and Polish spaces): for π∈U(α,β) there is a family (πx​)x​ of probability measures, unique for α-almost every x, with ∫fdπ=∫(∫f(x,y)dπx​(y))dα(x): “draw X∼α, then Y∼πX​”.
  • Conditional expectation: E[Y∣X]=m(X) with m(x)=∫ydπx​(y). It is a random variable (a function of X), with E[E[Y∣X]]=E[Y] (tower rule) and Var(Y)=E[Var(Y∣X)]+Var(E[Y∣X]).
  • Best prediction: m minimises E∥Y−h(X)∥2 over all functions h.
Worked example — the glued plan of Lesson 3

In the gluing example the glued plan between x∈{0,2} and z∈{1,3} is π=(3/81/8​1/83/8​) (rows x, columns z).

  • Given X=0: Z=1 with probability 1/23/8​=43​, Z=3 with probability 41​, so E[Z∣X=0]=1.5. Given X=2: E[Z∣X=2]=41​+49​=2.5.
  • Tower rule: 21​⋅1.5+21​⋅2.5=2=E[Z]. Variances: Var(Z)=1=EVar(Z∣X)0.75​​+VarE[Z∣X]0.25​​.
  • The map x↦E[Z∣X=x] (0↦1.5, 2↦2.5) is the barycentric projection of the plan: a map built from a plan by averaging where each point sends its mass (OT4ML Def. 12.32, p. 281).
Why the conditional expectation is the best prediction

Write Y−h(X)=(Y−m(X))+(m(X)−h(X)) and expand the square. The cross term vanishes: conditioning on X, E[⟨Y−m(X),m(X)−h(X)⟩∣X]=⟨E[Y∣X]−m(X),m(X)−h(X)⟩=0. Hence

E∥Y−h(X)∥2=E∥Y−m(X)∥2+E∥m(X)−h(X)∥2 ≥ E∥Y−m(X)∥2,

with equality iff h=m almost surely: m is the orthogonal projection of Y on the functions of X (Pythagoras in L2).

Pitfall — conditioning on an event of probability zero

When X has a density, P(X=x)=0 and “P(Y∈B∣X=x)=P(Y∈B,X=x)/P(X=x)” is 0/0. The conditional law is then defined through densities or disintegration, and only for almost every x. Also, P(Y∣X) and P(X∣Y) are different objects: for a plan, “where does x send its mass” versus “where does the mass arriving at y come from”.

In machine learning — regression with the squared loss learns a conditional expectation

A network trained with the loss E∥fθ​(X)−Y∥2 tends to E[Y∣X], the best predictor above. Flow matching uses exactly this: the velocity field that transports noise to data is vt​(z)=E[X1​−X0​∣Xt​=z] for Xt​=(1−t)X0​+tX1​, the average velocity of all straight paths through z, learned by least squares (OT4ML Prop. 16.3, p. 408–409). Denoisers are conditional expectations too: Tweedie’s identity E[W∣W+σε=z]=z+σ2∇logρσ​(z) links them to the score used by diffusion models (OT4ML Prop. 16.6, p. 411).

For the optimal plan P⋆=(1/40​1/41/2​) between a=(21​,21​) and b=(41​,43​) on {0,1} (above), what is the law of Y given X=0, and the barycentric projection x↦E[Y∣X=x]?

Answer

Row X=0 has mass 21​, split equally: given X=0, Y=0 or Y=1 with probability 21​ each, so E[Y∣X=0]=21​. Row X=1 sends everything to 1: E[Y∣X=1]=1. The plan splits the mass at 0 (it is not a map), and its barycentric projection 0↦21​, 1↦1 averages the destinations.

Convergence of random variables and of measures; law of large numbers, central limit theorem#

Used in Lesson 3 (weak convergence, CLT, total variation), Lesson 5 (Monte Carlo over directions), Lesson 7 (sample complexity of OT), Lesson 8 (particle approximations).

Random variables can be close in several senses: realisation by realisation, with high probability, on average, or only through their laws. For measures, the useful notion compares averages of bounded continuous functions.

Definitions weak convergence: OT4ML Def. 4.18, p. 81
  • Almost surely: Xn​(ω)→X(ω) for all ω outside a null set. In probability: P(∥Xn​−X∥>ε)→0 for every ε>0. In Lp: E∥Xn​−X∥p→0.
  • Weak convergence of measures: αn​⇀α iff ∫φdαn​→∫φdα for every bounded continuous φ. In law: Xn​→X in law iff their laws converge weakly. Only the laws matter: the variables need not live on the same probability space.
  • Implications: almost surely ⇒ in probability ⇒ in law, and Lp⇒ in probability (Markov’s inequality).
Law of large numbers and central limit theorem OT4ML Prop. 10.1, p. 195; Remark 4.23, p. 82

Let X1​,X2​,… be i.i.d. with law α, mean m and covariance Σ, and Xˉn​=n1​∑i≤n​Xi​.

  • LLN: Xˉn​→m almost surely (finite mean suffices). For measures: the empirical measure α^n​=n1​∑i​δXi​​ converges weakly to α almost surely, and Wp​(α^n​,α)→0 if α∈Pp​.
  • CLT: n​(Xˉn​−m)→N(0,Σ) in law (finite variance needed). So the error of an average of n samples is of order σ/n​, in any dimension.
Worked example — one hundred dice

A die has mean 3.5 and variance 1235​. The mean Xˉ100​ of 100 dice has standard deviation 35/12​/10≈0.171. The CLT predicts P(​Xˉ100​−3.5​≤0.34)≈P(∣Z∣≤1.99)≈0.954. The exact value, obtained by convolving the law of one die 100 times, is 0.957 (the normal approximation with the usual continuity correction also gives 0.957). The error of an average scales like 1/n​: four times more dice, half the error.

In law but not in probability: if X∼N(0,1) and Xn​=−X, then Xn​ has the law of X for every n (convergence in law is trivial), but ∣Xn​−X∣=2∣X∣ does not go to 0.

Pitfalls
  • Weak convergence does not imply convergence of moments: mass can escape to infinity (Lesson 3). That is why Wp​-convergence on Rd is “weak convergence + convergence of p-th moments”.
  • The CLT needs a finite variance: averages of Cauchy variables do not concentrate at all.
  • The n​1​ rate is for averages of a fixed function. Distances between an empirical measure and its law are slower: Wp​(α^n​,α) decays like n−1/d in dimension d>2p (the curse of dimensionality, OT4ML p. 198), while MMD and sliced distances keep n−1/2 (OT4ML Prop. 10.11, p. 203; Thm. 10.16, p. 207).
In machine learning — minibatches are Monte Carlo averages

The loss on a minibatch of size B is an empirical average of per-example losses: it is an unbiased estimate of the population loss, and by the CLT its fluctuation is of order σ/B​. Going from B=64 to B=256 halves the gradient noise. An OT loss between two minibatches is not an average of per-example terms: it is noisy and also biased, which is one reason why Lesson 7 studies entropic and debiased versions with better sample complexity.

2. Distributions on the line#

On the real line a distribution is described by its cumulative distribution function, or equivalently by its quantile function; matching equal quantile levels — sorting — solves optimal transport for every convex cost.

Cumulative distribution function and quantile function#

Used in Lesson 1 (the optimal map T=Cβ−1​∘Cα​), Lesson 2 (1D discrete transport), Lesson 3 (Wp​ on the line, Riemann sums, barycenters), Lesson 5 (sliced OT: every projection is a 1D problem).

The cumulative distribution function (CDF) accumulates the mass from left to right. The quantile function answers the reverse question: where has a fraction t of the mass been accumulated? It is the inverse of the CDF with the two axes swapped — with a precise convention where the CDF jumps or is flat.

In the course OT4ML Def. 2.39 and Prop. 2.40, p. 37

For α∈M1+​(R), the CDF and the quantile function (generalized inverse) are

Cα​(x)=α((−∞,x]),Cα−1​(t)=inf{x∈R: Cα​(x)≥t},t∈(0,1).

One has (Cα−1​)#​U(0,1)=α. If α has no atoms, then (Cα​)#​α=U(0,1).

Cα​
Non-decreasing, right-continuous, from 0 (at −∞) to 1 (at +∞). It jumps by α({x}) at each atom x, and is flat on intervals that carry no mass.
Cα−1​
Non-decreasing and left-continuous. Atoms of α (jumps of Cα​) become flat pieces of Cα−1​; gaps of the support (flat pieces of Cα​) become jumps of Cα−1​.
the key equivalence
Cα−1​(t)≤x⟺t≤Cα​(x), for t∈(0,1) and x∈R. Everything else follows from it.
(Cα−1​)#​U=α
Inverse transform sampling: if U is uniform on (0,1), then Cα−1​(U)∼α.
Worked example — the measure of the figure

For α=41​δ0​+21​U[1,2]+41​δ3​:

Cα​(x)=⎩⎨⎧​041​41​+2x−1​43​1​x<00≤x<11≤x<22≤x<3x≥3​Cα−1​(t)=⎩⎨⎧​01+2(t−41​)3​0<t≤41​41​<t≤43​43​<t<1.​
  • Cα−1​(0.1)=0 although Cα​(0)=0.25>0.1: the level falls inside the jump of the atom at 0, like every level in (0,41​].
  • Cα−1​(0.3)=1.1 and Cα​(1.1)=0.3: on the uniform part the two functions are true inverses. But Cα−1​(0.75)=2 and Cα−1​(0.8)=3: the quantile function jumps over the gap (2,3).
  • Sampling: Cα−1​(U)=0 exactly when U≤41​, an event of probability 41​=α({0}) (on 200000 simulated uniforms, the frequencies of “=0”, “=3” and “∈[1,1.5]” are all within 0.003 of 41​).
Proof of the key equivalence and of inverse transform sampling
  1. If t≤Cα​(x), then x belongs to the set {x′: Cα​(x′)≥t}, so its infimum satisfies Cα−1​(t)≤x.Definition of an infimum.
  2. Conversely, the set {x′: Cα​(x′)≥t} is an interval [q,∞) that contains its left end q=Cα−1​(t): it is an interval because Cα​ is non-decreasing, and it contains q because Cα​ is right-continuous. So Cα−1​(t)≤x implies x∈[q,∞), i.e. Cα​(x)≥t.Right-continuity is exactly what is needed.
  3. P(Cα−1​(U)≤x)=P(U≤Cα​(x))=Cα​(x).
    The equivalence, then P(U≤s)=s for s∈[0,1]. Two laws with the same CDF are equal, so Cα−1​(U)∼α.

Interactive figure (needs JavaScript).

What to look at: move the level t. On the CDF (top), the green line at height t stops at the first point where the CDF reaches t: that point is C−1(t), also marked on the quantile function (bottom); every level below 41​ stops on the jump at 0. Then press “Draw 40 samples”: uniform levels (grey lines) become the samples C−1(U) (grey dots under the axis). They pile up where the CDF is steep, and each atom catches, on average, a fraction of the levels equal to its mass (the readout counts them). For the 5-point measure, C−1 is a staircase and sampling picks one of the five points uniformly.

Pitfalls
  • Cα−1​ is not an inverse function in general: Cα​(Cα−1​(t))≥t, strict inside a jump; Cα−1​(Cα​(x))≤x, strict inside a gap (in the example Cα−1​(Cα​(0.5))=Cα−1​(0.25)=0<0.5).
  • (Cα​)#​α is uniform only if α has no atoms (Exercise 11 of the Lesson 1 sheet). Other texts use P(X<x) or inf{x: C(x)>t}: they differ at countably many points only, which changes no integral.
In machine learning — sampling and histogram matching

Inverse transform sampling is how libraries turn uniform random numbers into other laws when C−1 is explicit: for the exponential law C−1(u)=−log(1−u), so C−1(0.5)=log2≈0.693 is its median. Matching quantiles is also a classical preprocessing: histogram equalization replaces each pixel intensity x by Cβ−1​(Cα​(x)), so that the output histogram is the target β (OT4ML §1.1, Fig. 1.3, p. 12); colour transfer does it channel by channel, and quantile normalization does it for gene-expression profiles. This map is exactly the optimal transport map on the line (§9).

For the empirical measure of the three points 2,−1,0.5, compute C−1(0.5) and C−1(31​).

Answer

Sort: −1≤0.5≤2, each with mass 31​. The quantile function is the staircase C−1(t)=x(⌈3t⌉)​. So C−1(0.5)=x(2)​=0.5 (the median), and C−1(31​)=x(1)​=−1: at the level t=31​ exactly, C(−1)=31​≥t already, and the infimum convention picks −1 (just above, C−1(0.34)=0.5).

Sorting, ranks and monotone rearrangement#

Used in Lesson 1 (discrete Monge on the line: sort and match), Lesson 2 (the north-west corner rule for unequal weights), Lesson 3 (monotone plans in the examples), Lesson 5 (sliced OT sorts projected samples).

To pair n points with n points on a line at the smallest total cost, pair the smallest with the smallest, the second with the second, and so on. The reason: two pairs that cross can be uncrossed, and for a convex cost uncrossing never increases the cost.

In the course OT4ML Prop. 1.2, p. 9–10; Prop. 3.10, p. 55

Monotone matching. Let x1​,…,xn​ be pairwise distinct, y1​,…,yn​ pairwise distinct, and Cij​=h(xi​−yj​) with h strictly convex. The unique optimal assignment is the order-preserving permutation. If h is only convex, the sorted matching is still optimal, but other optimal matchings may exist.

Weighted sweep. For sorted weighted atoms x1​≤⋯≤xn​, y1​≤⋯≤ym​ and c(x,y)=h(x−y) with h convex, the north-west corner plan (fill the targets from left to right) is optimal; cost O(nlogn+mlogm) with the sorting.

rank
The rank of xi​ is its position after sorting. If σX​ and σY​ are the sorting permutations, the optimal matching sends xσX​(k)​ to yσY​(k)​ for each k, i.e. σ=σY​∘σX−1​.
Wp​ of point clouds
Wpp​(n1​∑i​δxi​​,n1​∑j​δyj​​)=n1​∑k​​x(k)​−y(k)​​p, where x(1)​≤⋯≤x(n)​ are the sorted values. It is the quantile formula of §9 for staircase quantile functions.
monotone rearrangement
For measures with densities the same rule reads T=Cβ−1​∘Cα​: the point at level t of α goes to the point at level t of β.
Worked example — all six permutations

For x=(0,1,3) and y=(1,2,5), the six matchings cost (squared distance) 6 (sorted), then 8, 18, 24, 26, and 30 (reversed). Hence W22​=36​=2. With the cost ∣x−y∣ the sorted matching costs 4, but so does the matching 0→2, 1→1, 3→5: for p=1 the optimum is not unique (W1​=34​).

Unsorted input: x=(3,0,1) and y=(5,2,1). Ranks of x: (3,1,2); of y: (3,2,1). Match equal ranks: 3→5, 0→1, 1→2 — the same pairs as above.

Proof: uncrossing two pairs

Take x<x′ matched to y′>y (a crossing), and set d=y′−y>0, D(s)=dh(s)−h(s−d)​, the slope of a chord of h of horizontal length d. Convexity of h makes D non-decreasing (strictly increasing if h is strictly convex). Then

[h(x−y′)+h(x′−y)]−[h(x−y)+h(x′−y′)]=d(D(x′−y)−D(x−y))≥0,

because x′−y>x−y; expand the four terms to check the identity. So swapping the two targets does not increase the cost (and strictly decreases it for strictly convex h). Repeating the swap removes every crossing; the only matching without crossing pairs equal ranks.

Pitfalls
  • For a concave cost (∣x−y∣p with p<1), sorting is not optimal: for x=(0,1), y=(1,2) and p=21​, the sorted matching costs 2 and the crossed one 2​≈1.41.
  • For p=1, ties are common (“book shifting”, OT4ML Example 1.3, p. 12): sorting gives an optimal matching, not the only one.
  • There is no order in dimension d≥2: sorting does not generalise; Brenier’s theorem (§9) replaces “increasing” by “gradient of a convex function”.
In machine learning — sliced Wasserstein losses

Sorting is the cheapest exact OT solver: O(nlogn). Sliced Wasserstein distances (Lesson 5, OT4ML Def. 11.23, p. 230) exploit it in high dimension: project both point clouds on random directions θ, sort the projections, and average the 1D costs n1​∑k​(⟨θ,x⟩(k)​−⟨θ,y⟩(k)​)2. The result is differentiable almost everywhere with respect to the points (the sorting permutation is locally constant), and is used as a training loss for generative models and to compare point clouds or feature distributions.

3. Linear algebra#

Symmetric positive matrices are stretchings along orthogonal axes; they have square roots, they are the covariances of Gaussian vectors, and permutation matrices are the corners of the set of doubly stochastic matrices.

Symmetric matrices, spectral theorem, positive (semi-)definite matrices#

Used in Lesson 1 (covariances; the Brenier map between Gaussians is a symmetric positive matrix), Lesson 3 (Gaussian barycenters; the sheet’s Gaussian couplings need block matrices ⪰0), Lesson 4 (Hessians of convex potentials), Lesson 7 (Gram matrices of kernels), Lesson 8 (strong convexity).

A symmetric matrix acts as a stretching along orthogonal axes: along each axis it multiplies lengths by an eigenvalue. It is positive semi-definite (PSD, S⪰0) when no axis is reversed, i.e. all the stretching factors are ≥0.

Spectral theorem and positivity (standard)
  • Spectral theorem. If S∈Rd×d is symmetric (S⊤=S), then S=UDU⊤ with U orthogonal (U⊤U=I, columns = orthonormal eigenvectors) and D=diag(λ1​,…,λd​) real.
  • PSD. The following are equivalent: x⊤Sx≥0 for all x; all λi​≥0; S=A⊤A for some matrix A. Positive definite (S≻0): x⊤Sx>0 for x=0, i.e. all λi​>0, i.e. S PSD and invertible.
  • Rayleigh bounds. λmin​∥x∥2≤x⊤Sx≤λmax​∥x∥2. Loewner order: A⪯B iff B−A⪰0.
  • 2×2 test. (ab​bc​)≻0 iff a>0 and ac−b2>0. In particular a covariance (σ12​c​cσ22​​) is PSD iff ∣c∣≤σ1​σ2​.
  • Schur complement. If A≻0, then (AB⊤​BC​)⪰0 iff C−B⊤A−1B⪰0.

Covariance matrices E[(X−m)(X−m)⊤] and Gram matrices (⟨xi​,xj​⟩)ij​ are PSD: x⊤E[(X−m)(X−m)⊤]x=E[⟨x,X−m⟩2]≥0.

Worked example
  • S=(21​12​): eigenvalues 3 (eigenvector (1,1)/2​) and 1 (eigenvector (1,−1)/2​). Directly: x⊤Sx=2x12​+2x1​x2​+2x22​=(x1​+x2​)2+x12​+x22​>0 for x=0.
  • (12​21​) has only positive entries but eigenvalues 3 and −1: with x=(1,−1), x⊤Sx=1−4+1=−2. Not PSD.
  • (1−1​−11​) has negative entries but eigenvalues 0 and 2: PSD (and singular).
  • Schur: (10.8​0.81​)⪰0 because 1−0.8⋅1−1⋅0.8=0.36≥0 (its eigenvalues are 0.2 and 1.8).
Proof of the equivalences

Write x=Uz (any x is of this form since U is invertible). Then x⊤Sx=z⊤U⊤UDU⊤Uz=z⊤Dz=∑i​λi​zi2​. This is ≥0 for all z iff all λi​≥0 (take z = a basis vector), and >0 for all z=0 iff all λi​>0. If all λi​≥0, then S=A⊤A with A=D1/2U⊤; conversely x⊤A⊤Ax=∥Ax∥2≥0. The Rayleigh bounds follow from λmin​∑zi2​≤∑λi​zi2​≤λmax​∑zi2​ and ∥z∥=∥x∥.

Pitfalls
  • The signs of the entries say nothing about definiteness (examples above).
  • The product of two symmetric positive matrices is in general not symmetric: diag(2,1)(21​12​)=(41​22​). This is why compositions of Brenier maps between Gaussians are in general not Brenier maps (OT4ML Example 2.43, p. 38), and why formulas such as the Bures distance use “sandwiches” A1/2BA1/2.
  • In kernel theory, “positive definite kernel” means that the Gram matrices are PSD (OT4ML p. 127).
In machine learning — PCA and curvature

Principal component analysis diagonalises the empirical covariance Σ^=UDU⊤: the columns of U are the principal axes and the eigenvalues the variances along them; keeping the k largest gives the best k-dimensional linear summary of the data. At a minimum of a smooth loss the Hessian is PSD, and the ratio λmax​/λmin​ of its eigenvalues (the condition number) governs the speed of gradient descent (§5).

Matrix square root, trace, determinant#

Used in Lesson 1 (Brenier map and W2​ between Gaussians, Bures distance), Lesson 3 (fixed-point equation of Gaussian barycenters), Lesson 7 (entropic OT between Gaussians), Lesson 8 (Gaussian flows).

Functions of a symmetric matrix act on its eigenvalues and keep its eigenvectors: same axes, transformed stretching factors. The square root is the most useful one.

Square root, trace, determinant (standard)
  • Every S⪰0 has a unique PSD square root: S1/2=UD1/2U⊤, the only R⪰0 with R2=S. More generally f(S)=Udiag(f(λi​))U⊤ (S−1/2, logS, eS…).
  • trS=∑i​λi​, detS=∏i​λi​. For any square A,B: tr(AB)=tr(BA), det(AB)=detAdetB, and AB and BA have the same eigenvalues. ⟨A,B⟩=tr(A⊤B)=∑ij​Aij​Bij​ is the Frobenius inner product.
  • 2×2 formula. For S⪰0 of size 2, not zero: S1/2=trS+2detS​​S+detS​I​.
In the course OT4ML Def. 2.55 and Prop. 2.56, p. 46

The Bures metric between PSD matrices is B(Σ,Λ)2=tr(Σ+Λ−2(Σ1/2ΛΣ1/2)1/2). For Σα​,Σβ​≻0 the optimal map from N(mα​,Σα​) to N(mβ​,Σβ​) is T(x)=mβ​+A(x−mα​) with A=Σα−1/2​(Σα1/2​Σβ​Σα1/2​)1/2Σα−1/2​, and W22​=∥mα​−mβ​∥2+B(Σα​,Σβ​)2.

Worked example
  • S=(21​12​) (λ=3,1): S1/2=21​(3​+13​−1​3​−13​+1​)≈(1.3660.366​0.3661.366​). The 2×2 formula gives the same: detS=3, trS=4, (S+3​I)/4+23​​.
  • The entrywise square root (2​1​12​​) is wrong: its square is (32.83​2.833​)=S.
  • Bures: B(I,S)2=tr(I+S−2S1/2)=2+4−2(3​+1)≈0.536. So W22​(N(0,I),N(0,S))≈0.536 (POT’s Gaussian solver agrees).
  • Non-commuting pair Σ=diag(1,4), Λ=S: the two sandwiches differ, (Σ1/2ΛΣ1/2)1/2≈(1.3280.486​0.4862.786​) and (Λ1/2ΣΛ1/2)1/2≈(1.4260.608​0.6082.689​), but they have the same trace 4.114. Hence B(Σ,Λ)2≈0.771 whichever order you use (the book and the board of Lesson 3 write the two orders).
Why the square root is unique, and where the 2×2 formula comes from

Uniqueness. Let R⪰0 with R2=S. If Rv=μv then Sv=μ2v: each eigenspace of R (eigenvalue μ≥0) lies in the eigenspace of S for μ2. Since μ↦μ2 is injective on [0,∞) and the eigenspaces of R fill the space, R acts as λ​ on the eigenspace of S for λ: R=UD1/2U⊤.

2×2 formula. Cayley–Hamilton for R=S1/2: R2−(trR)R+(detR)I=0, i.e. S+detS​I=(trR)R. And (trR)2=(λ1​​+λ2​​)2=trS+2detS​. Divide.

Same trace for the two sandwiches. Σ1/2ΛΣ1/2 and Λ1/2ΣΛ1/2 are of the form XX⊤ and X⊤X with X=Σ1/2Λ1/2: they have the same eigenvalues, hence their square roots have the same eigenvalues and the same trace.

Pitfalls
  • (AB)1/2=A1/2B1/2 unless A and B commute. “Average the square roots” is right for commuting covariances only (Lesson 3).
  • Square roots are not unique without the condition R⪰0: −S1/2 and Udiag(±λi​​)U⊤ also square to S.
  • Some codes compute tr((ΣΛ)1/2) with a general matrix square root of the non-symmetric matrix ΣΛ. The trace is right (ΣΛ is similar to Σ1/2ΛΣ1/2), but the computation can return small imaginary parts that must be discarded.
In machine learning — the Fréchet Inception Distance

The FID used to evaluate image generators (GANs, diffusion models) embeds real and generated images with a fixed network, fits a Gaussian N(m,Σ) to each cloud of features, and reports W22​ between the two Gaussians: ∥m1​−m2​∥2+tr(Σ1​+Σ2​−2(Σ11/2​Σ2​Σ11/2​)1/2), exactly the formula above (OT4ML Example 7.14, p. 129).

Compute W22​(N(0,diag(1,4)), N(0,diag(4,1))).

Answer

Diagonal matrices commute, so the Bures term is computed eigenvalue by eigenvalue: B2=∑i​(λi​​−μi​​)2=(1−2)2+(2−1)2=2. The means are equal, so W22​=2. (The optimal map is diag(2,21​): stretch the first axis, shrink the second.)

Gaussian vectors: densities, affine maps, covariances#

Used in Lesson 1 (OT between Gaussians), Lesson 3 (Gaussian barycenters, Gaussian couplings), Lesson 5 (projections of Gaussians), Lesson 6 (Gaussian noise as the source of generative flows), Lesson 7 (entropic OT between Gaussians), Lesson 8 (Ornstein–Uhlenbeck, diffusion models, linear dynamics).

A Gaussian vector is a standard Gaussian cloud Z∼N(0,I), stretched by a matrix and shifted: X=m+AZ. Its level sets are ellipsoids, and everything about it is determined by its mean m and its covariance Σ=AA⊤.

Facts about N(m,Σ) affine maps: OT4ML Prop. 2.54, p. 46
  • Density (if Σ≻0): ρ(x)=(2π)−d/2(detΣ)−1/2exp(−21​(x−m)⊤Σ−1(x−m)). The quantity (x−m)⊤Σ−1(x−m) is the squared Mahalanobis distance.
  • Construction: X=m+Σ1/2Z with Z∼N(0,I) (any A with AA⊤=Σ works).
  • Affine maps: if X∼N(m,Σ) then BX+c∼N(Bm+c,BΣB⊤). In particular every projection ⟨θ,X⟩∼N(⟨θ,m⟩,θ⊤Σθ).
  • Sums: independent N(m1​,Σ1​) and N(m2​,Σ2​) add up to N(m1​+m2​,Σ1​+Σ2​). Second moment: E∥X∥2=∥m∥2+trΣ.
  • For a jointly Gaussian vector, uncorrelated components are independent.
Worked example — Σ=(21​12​), m=0
  • The ellipse {x⊤Σ−1x=1} has half-axes 3​≈1.73 along (1,1)/2​ and 1 along (1,−1)/2​. The density at 0 is 1/(2π3​)≈0.0919.
  • Σ−1=31​(2−1​−12​): the point (1,1) has squared Mahalanobis distance 32​, the point (1,−1) has 2. Same Euclidean norm, but the first lies along the long axis: it is “closer” for the Gaussian.
  • Projections: variance 2 along (1,0), 3 along (1,1)/2​, 1 along (1,−1)/2​ — the eigenvalues are the extreme projected variances.
  • With mean m=(1,2): E∥X∥2=5+4=9.
Mean and covariance of an affine image

E[BX+c]=BE[X]+c by linearity. Cov(BX+c)=E[B(X−m)(X−m)⊤B⊤]=BΣB⊤. That BX+c is again Gaussian follows from the construction: BX+c=(Bm+c)+(BA)Z is an affine image of a standard Gaussian. If B is invertible you can also check it with the push-forward density formula (§1).

Pitfalls
  • Gaussian marginals do not make a Gaussian vector: if X∼N(0,1) and Y=SX with an independent random sign S, then Y∼N(0,1) and Cov(X,Y)=0, but X+Y=0 with probability 21​ — not Gaussian, and X,Y are not independent.
  • Notation: N(m,σ2) is written with the variance in this course; some codes take the standard deviation.
  • If Σ is singular the Gaussian has no density: it lives on an affine subspace.
In machine learning — the reparametrization trick of VAEs

A variational auto-encoder outputs, for an input x, a mean μϕ​(x) and standard deviations σϕ​(x), and samples the code as z=μϕ​(x)+σϕ​(x)⊙ε with ε∼N(0,I). This is the affine push-forward above: z∼N(μϕ​(x),diag(σϕ​(x)2)), and since the randomness sits in ε, the gradient of the loss with respect to ϕ passes through the sampling step. The KL term of the VAE loss is the Gaussian KL of §6.

Permutation matrices and doubly stochastic matrices#

Used in Lesson 1 (the assignment problem), Lesson 2 (Birkhoff–von Neumann: for uniform weights the Kantorovich LP has a permutation among its solutions), Lesson 7 (Sinkhorn scales a positive matrix to prescribed row and column sums).

A permutation matrix has exactly one 1 in each row and each column: it pairs indices. A doubly stochastic matrix is a “fractional pairing”: rows and columns sum to 1. The second notion is the convex relaxation of the first, and the relaxation is exact.

In the course OT4ML Def. 3.11–3.12, p. 56; Thm. 3.17, p. 57; Cor. 3.20, p. 58

For σ∈Perm(n), (Pσ​)ij​=1 if j=σ(i) and 0 otherwise. The Birkhoff polytope is Bn​={P∈R+n×n​: P1n​=1n​, P⊤1n​=1n​}, and U(1n​/n,1n​/n)=Bn​/n.

Birkhoff–von Neumann: the extreme points of Bn​ are exactly the permutation matrices. Every P∈Bn​ is a convex combination of at most (n−1)2+1 permutation matrices.

Worked example — decomposing a doubly stochastic matrix

Let C be the cyclic shift (C12​=C23​=C31​=1). Then

D=​0.50.20.3​0.30.50.2​0.20.30.5​​=0.5I+0.3C+0.2C2.

Greedy algorithm: find a permutation inside the support of D (here I), subtract the smallest of its entries (0.5) times it, repeat: it finds the three terms. For n=3 the polytope has dimension (n−1)2=4, hence at most 5 terms. The decomposition is not unique: the matrix with all entries 31​ equals 31​(I+C+C2) and also 31​ times the sum of the three transpositions.

Idea of the proof of Birkhoff–von Neumann

Permutations are extreme: entries of a doubly stochastic matrix lie in [0,1]; if Pσ​=21​(Q+R) with Q,R∈Bn​, every entry 0 or 1 of Pσ​ forces the same entry in Q and R, so Q=R=Pσ​.

Nothing else is extreme: if P has a fractional entry, its row and its column contain another fractional entry; following fractional entries alternately along rows and columns gives a cycle. Adding ±ε alternately along the cycle keeps all row and column sums and writes P as the midpoint of two different doubly stochastic matrices (OT4ML p. 57–58).

Pitfalls
  • Doubly stochastic is not symmetric (D above is not), and a coupling between uniform measures is P/n, not P.
  • Birkhoff’s theorem is about uniform weights and n=m. For general histograms an optimal plan need not be a permutation (mass may have to split); one can only guarantee a solution with at most n+m−1 nonzero entries (§5).
In machine learning — matchings inside models

Set-prediction models such as the DETR object detector compare a set of predicted boxes with the set of ground-truth boxes by first solving an assignment problem (Hungarian algorithm), then applying the loss to matched pairs. When a differentiable relaxation is needed, the permutation is replaced by a doubly stochastic matrix obtained by Sinkhorn scaling of e−C/ε (Lesson 7); when the optimal permutation is unique, this matrix tends to its permutation matrix as ε→0.

4. Analysis#

Inequalities to bound integrals, Lipschitz functions and compactness to guarantee that optimizers exist, the Jacobian to change variables, and the calculus of vector fields — divergence, ODE flows, continuity equation — to describe mass in motion.

Norms and inequalities: Cauchy–Schwarz, Hölder, Minkowski, Jensen#

Used in Lesson 3 (Minkowski in the triangle inequality of Wp​, Jensen in Wp​≤Wq​), Lesson 4 (duality bounds), Lesson 7 (Jensen gives KL≥0), Lesson 8 (Cauchy–Schwarz in energy estimates).

A norm measures size; the Lp norms of a function weigh its large values more and more as p grows. Four inequalities do almost all the work: Cauchy–Schwarz and Hölder bound a product, Minkowski is the triangle inequality of Lp, and Jensen says that a convex function of an average is below the average of the function.

The four inequalities (standard)

Let α be a measure, ∥f∥p​=(∫∣f∣pdα)1/p for 1≤p<∞ and ∥f∥∞​=sup∣f∣ (for vectors, α = counting measure).

  • Cauchy–Schwarz: ∣⟨u,v⟩∣≤∥u∥∥v∥, with equality iff u and v are collinear.
  • Hölder: ∫∣fg∣dα≤∥f∥p​∥g∥q​ when p1​+q1​=1 (p=q=2 is Cauchy–Schwarz).
  • Minkowski (p≥1): ∥f+g∥p​≤∥f∥p​+∥g∥p​.
  • Jensen: if α is a probability measure and φ is convex, φ(∫fdα)≤∫φ∘fdα, i.e. φ(EU)≤Eφ(U). Reversed for concave φ.

Consequences: on a probability space ∥f∥p​≤∥f∥q​ for p≤q (Jensen with φ(s)=sq/p); Young’s inequality ab≤pap​+qbq​ for a,b≥0.

Worked example
  • u=(1,2,3), v=(4,−5,6): ⟨u,v⟩=12≤∥u∥∥v∥=14​77​≈32.8. Hölder with (p,q)=(1,∞): ∑∣ui​vi​∣=32≤∥u∥1​∥v∥∞​=6⋅6=36. Minkowski: ∥u+v∥≈10.72≤∥u∥+∥v∥≈12.52.
  • U uniform on {1,2,3}, φ(s)=s2: φ(EU)=4≤Eφ(U)=314​≈4.67; the gap is Var(U)=32​. The norms ∥U∥1​=2, ∥U∥2​≈2.16, ∥U∥3​≈2.29, ∥U∥∞​=3 increase with p. With the concave log: ElogU≈0.597≤logEU≈0.693.
Proofs of Cauchy–Schwarz and Jensen

Cauchy–Schwarz. For every real t, 0≤∥u+tv∥2=∥u∥2+2t⟨u,v⟩+t2∥v∥2. A quadratic polynomial in t that never takes negative values has a non-positive discriminant: 4⟨u,v⟩2−4∥u∥2∥v∥2≤0.

Jensen. Let m=EU. A convex φ lies above a supporting line at m: φ(u)≥φ(m)+s(u−m) for all u, for some slope s (the derivative if it exists). Take expectations: Eφ(U)≥φ(m)+s(EU−m)=φ(m). This is the dashed tangent of the figure.

Hölder follows by integrating Young’s inequality ∣fg∣≤p∣f∣p​+q∣g∣q​ after normalising ∥f∥p​=∥g∥q​=1; Minkowski by applying Hölder to ∣f+g∣p≤∣f∣∣f+g∣p−1+∣g∣∣f+g∣p−1.

Pitfalls
  • Minkowski is false for p<1 (counterexample in Lesson 3): that is why Wp​ needs p≥1.
  • Jensen needs weights summing to 1, and its direction depends on convexity: ElogU≤logEU, but EU2≥(EU)2.
In machine learning — the evidence lower bound (ELBO)

For a latent-variable model pθ​(x,z) and any distribution q(z), Jensen with the concave log gives

logpθ​(x)=logEz∼q​[q(z)pθ​(x,z)​] ≥ Ez∼q​[logpθ​(x,z)−logq(z)]=ELBO(q,θ).

VAEs and variational inference maximise this lower bound; the gap is exactly KL(q∣pθ​(⋅∣x)) (§6). Cauchy–Schwarz is also why cosine similarities ⟨u,v⟩/(∥u∥∥v∥) between embeddings lie in [−1,1].

Continuous and Lipschitz functions, compactness#

Used in Lesson 3 (Lipschitz test functions; existence of optimal plans), Lesson 4 (W1​ as a supremum over 1-Lipschitz functions; c-transforms inherit the regularity of the cost; Arzelà–Ascoli gives optimal potentials; Wasserstein GANs), Lessons 6 and 8 (Lipschitz velocity fields give well-defined flows).

A Lipschitz function cannot change faster than a fixed multiple of the distance travelled: its graph has bounded slopes. Compactness is the property that makes minimisation problems have solutions: every sequence has a convergent subsequence, so a minimising sequence has a limit.

Definitions Lipschitz constant: OT4ML Def. 6.16, p. 120
  • f is L-Lipschitz if ∣f(x)−f(y)∣≤Ld(x,y) for all x,y. The smallest such L is Lip(f)=supx=y​d(x,y)∣f(x)−f(y)∣​. For f of class C1 on a convex set, Lip(f)=sup∥∇f∥.
  • A metric space is compact if every sequence has a convergent subsequence. In Rd: closed and bounded.
The facts used in the course (standard)
  1. Weierstrass. A continuous (or just lower semi-continuous) function on a compact set attains its minimum. This is how the existence of optimal plans is proved: the set of couplings is compact for weak convergence and the cost is lower semi-continuous (OT4ML Prop. 3.34, p. 66).
  2. Heine. A continuous function on a compact metric space is uniformly continuous.
  3. Envelopes. An infimum (or supremum) of L-Lipschitz functions, if finite, is L-Lipschitz. This is why c-transforms are as regular as the cost (OT4ML Prop. 5.10, p. 99).
  4. Arzelà–Ascoli. On a compact metric space, a family of functions that is uniformly bounded and equicontinuous (for instance: all L-Lipschitz functions with ∣f∣≤M) is relatively compact for the sup norm: every sequence has a uniformly convergent subsequence.
  5. The same for measures (Prokhorov). On a compact space every sequence of probability measures has a weakly convergent subsequence (OT4ML Remark 7.22, p. 132).
Worked example
  • ∣x∣ and sinx are 1-Lipschitz on R. x2 is 4-Lipschitz on [−2,2] but not Lipschitz on R. x​ is continuous on [0,1] but not Lipschitz: 0.010.01​−0​=10, and the ratio blows up near 0.
  • Envelope: with x=(0,1,3) and f=(0,0.5,1), the lower envelope g(y)=mini​(∣y−xi​∣−fi​) takes the values 0,−0.5,0,−1,0 at y=0,1,2,3,4 — a 1-Lipschitz zigzag, as fact 3 predicts. (It is a discrete c-transform for c=∣x−y∣, §9.)
  • No compactness, no convergent subsequence: fn​(x)=sin(nx) on [0,π] are bounded by 1 but Lip(fn​)=n; no subsequence converges uniformly. Normalised 1-Lipschitz functions on [0,1] (f(0)=0), on the contrary, form a compact family.
Proof of fact 3 (envelopes of Lipschitz functions)

Let g=infk​fk​ with each fk​ L-Lipschitz. For all x,y and k: g(x)≤fk​(x)≤fk​(y)+Ld(x,y). Take the infimum over k: g(x)≤g(y)+Ld(x,y). Exchange x and y: ∣g(x)−g(y)∣≤Ld(x,y).

Pitfalls
  • Without compactness a minimum may not exist: e−x on R has infimum 0, never attained.
  • Arzelà–Ascoli needs a uniform bound. Kantorovich potentials are defined up to an additive constant, so one normalises them, e.g. f(x0​)=0, before extracting a subsequence (OT4ML, proof of Prop. 5.5, p. 97).
  • The Lipschitz constant depends on the distance used on the space.
In machine learning — Lipschitz critics in Wasserstein GANs

By Kantorovich–Rubinstein duality (Lesson 4), W1​(α,β)=supLip(f)≤1​∫fd(α−β): a Wasserstein GAN trains a critic network f to maximise Ef(real)−Ef(generated) under a Lipschitz constraint. In practice: weight clipping (a crude proxy, OT4ML Remark 7.26, p. 135), a gradient penalty (∥∇f∥−1)2 at random points, or spectral normalisation, which uses that a linear layer x↦Wx has Lipschitz constant ∥W∥op​ (largest singular value), ReLU is 1-Lipschitz, and Lipschitz constants multiply under composition.

Change of variables in integrals, Jacobian determinant#

Used in Lesson 1 (densities of push-forwards; the Monge–Ampère equation), Lesson 6 (densities along a flow), Lesson 8 (entropy along a flow), and normalizing flows.

A smooth map distorts volumes: near x it acts like its Jacobian matrix JT​(x)=T′(x), which sends a small cube of volume hd to a small parallelepiped of volume ∣detJT​(x)∣hd. Integrals change accordingly.

Change of variables (standard)

If T:U→V is a C1 diffeomorphism between open sets of Rd and g≥0 (or integrable),

∫V​g(y)dy=∫U​g(T(x))∣detJT​(x)∣dx.

Linear case: T(x)=Ax multiplies all volumes by ∣detA∣. Applied to densities this gives the push-forward formula of §1; for a Brenier map T=∇φ (so JT​=∇2φ⪰0) it gives the Monge–Ampère equation ρα​(x)=det(∇2φ(x))ρβ​(∇φ(x)).

Worked example
  • Polar coordinates T(r,θ)=(rcosθ,rsinθ) have detJT​=r, so ∫R2​e−∥x∥2/2dx=∫02π​∫0∞​e−r2/2rdrdθ=2π: the normalising constant of the 2D Gaussian.
  • A=(20​11​) has detA=2: the unit square becomes a parallelogram of area 2, and the uniform law on the square is pushed to the uniform law on the parallelogram, with density 21​.
  • Log-normal: if X∼N(0,1), Y=eX has density ϕ(logy)/y (here T−1(y)=logy, (T−1)′(y)=1/y); at y=2: ≈0.157.
Why ∣detJ∣

Cut U into small cubes of side h. On the cube at x, T(x+u)≈T(x)+JT​(x)u: the cube is mapped to (almost) the parallelepiped spanned by the columns of hJT​(x), whose volume is ∣detJT​(x)∣hd. Summing g(T(x))×volume over the image cubes gives a Riemann sum of ∫V​g on one side and of ∫U​g∘T∣detJT​∣ on the other. The rigorous proof controls the error of the linear approximation uniformly.

Pitfalls
  • Do not forget the absolute value: a reflection has det=−1 but preserves volumes.
  • In the target density, the Jacobian is evaluated at the preimage: ρβ​(y)=ρα​(T−1y)/​detJT​(T−1y)​, not at y.
In machine learning — normalizing flows

A normalizing flow is an invertible network fθ​ sending data x to a latent z=fθ​(x)∼N(0,I). Its likelihood is computed by the change of variables, logpθ​(x)=logϕ(fθ​(x))+log∣detJfθ​​(x)∣, and the model is trained by maximum likelihood. Layers are designed so that the determinant is cheap (triangular Jacobians: log∣det∣ is a sum of logs of diagonal entries). One-dimensional check: for x=1+2z, logp(3)=logϕ(1)−log2≈−1.419−0.693=−2.112, which is indeed log of the N(1,4) density at 3. Continuous-time flows replace logdet by an integral of the divergence (below).

Gradient, divergence, Laplacian, integration by parts#

Used in Lesson 6 (the continuity equation; Benamou–Brenier velocities are gradients), Lesson 8 (Wasserstein gradient flows ∂t​ρ=div(ρ∇δρδF​), Fokker–Planck), score matching.

The gradient points uphill. The divergence of a vector field measures how much it spreads out from a point: positive at a source, negative at a sink, zero for a rotation. The Laplacian is the divergence of the gradient: it compares a function with its local averages. Integration by parts moves a derivative from one factor to the other, at the price of a sign and a boundary term.

Definitions and formulas (standard)

For f:Rd→R and a vector field v:Rd→Rd:

​∇f=(∂1​f,…,∂d​f),divv=i=1∑d​∂i​vi​,Δf=div∇f=i=1∑d​∂ii​f,div(fv)=⟨∇f,v⟩+fdivv(product rule).​

Divergence theorem: ∫Ω​divv=∫∂Ω​⟨v,n⟩ (outward normal n): total spreading inside = flux through the boundary. Integration by parts:

∫Ω​fdivv=−∫Ω​⟨∇f,v⟩+∫∂Ω​f⟨v,n⟩,∫fΔg=−∫⟨∇f,∇g⟩on Rd,

where on Rd the boundary terms vanish when the functions decay at infinity. In 1D: ∫fg′=[fg]−∫f′g.

Worked example
  • v(x)=x in R2 (uniform expansion): divv=2. On the disk of radius r: ∫divv=2πr2, and the flux through the circle is ⟨v,n⟩=r times the length 2πr. Equal.
  • The rotation v(x)=(−x2​,x1​) has divv=0: it moves mass without compressing it.
  • Standard Gaussian density ρ in Rd: ∇ρ=−xρ and Δρ=(∥x∥2−d)ρ (at x=(1,0.5) in 2D: ≈−0.0639, confirmed by finite differences).
  • Stein’s identity E[Zf(Z)]=E[f′(Z)] for Z∼N(0,1): integrate by parts with ρ′=−xρ. With f(z)=z3: E[Z4]=3=E[3Z2].
Integration by parts from the divergence theorem

Apply the divergence theorem to the field fv and use the product rule div(fv)=⟨∇f,v⟩+fdivv: ∫Ω​⟨∇f,v⟩+∫Ω​fdivv=∫∂Ω​f⟨v,n⟩. With v=∇g you get Green’s formula. For Stein: E[f′(Z)]=∫f′ρ=−∫fρ′=∫f(z)zρ(z)dz=E[Zf(Z)].

Pitfalls
  • Signs: −Δ is the positive operator (∫f(−Δf)=∫∥∇f∥2≥0).
  • On a bounded domain the boundary terms do not vanish by themselves; in dynamic OT one imposes no flux through the boundary, ⟨ρv,n⟩=0 (OT4ML Def. 14.1, p. 328–329).
  • The divergence of a matrix field is taken row by row.
In machine learning — score matching

Diffusion models need the score ∇logp of the data law, which is unknown. Integration by parts removes it: Ep​∥sθ​(X)−∇logp(X)∥2=Ep​[∥sθ​(X)∥2+2divsθ​(X)]+const (Hyvärinen’s score matching), a loss that only needs samples of p. Its denoising variant is the training loss of diffusion models (OT4ML §16.1, p. 407).

Ordinary differential equations and flows of vector fields#

Used in Lesson 3 (particles moving along straight lines), Lesson 6 (dynamic OT; flow matching samples by integrating an ODE), Lesson 8 (gradient flows, particle systems, training of two-layer networks).

A vector field vt​(x) prescribes a velocity at each point and time. A particle released at x0​ follows it; the flow map Tt​ sends each starting point to its position at time t. Moving all the particles of a measure α0​ gives the measures αt​=(Tt​)#​α0​.

Cauchy–Lipschitz (Picard–Lindelöf) and consequences (standard)

If (t,x)↦vt​(x) is continuous and L-Lipschitz in x, then for every x0​ the problem x˙(t)=vt​(x(t)), x(0)=x0​ has a unique solution for all t∈[0,1]. Consequently:

  • the flow map Tt​ is a bijection (a diffeomorphism if v is C1); trajectories never cross;
  • Grönwall: ∥Tt​(x)−Tt​(y)∥≤eLt∥x−y∥;
  • linear fields: x˙=Ax gives x(t)=etAx0​;
  • gradient flows x˙=−∇f(x) decrease f: dtd​f(x(t))=−∥∇f(x(t))∥2≤0;
  • Euler’s scheme xk+1​=xk​+hvtk​​(xk​) converges with an error O(h) (gradient descent is Euler’s scheme for the gradient flow).
Worked example
  • x˙=−x, x(0)=1: x(1)=e−1≈0.368. Euler with step h gives (1−h)1/h: 0.25 for h=0.5, 0.349 for h=0.1, 0.366 for h=0.01; the errors 0.118, 0.019, 0.0018 shrink like h.
  • The flow map of x˙=−x is Tt​(x)=e−tx: it pushes N(0,1) to N(0,e−2t).
  • Non-Lipschitz field: x˙=∣x∣​, x(0)=0 has two solutions, x≡0 and x(t)=t2/4. Superlinear field: x˙=x2, x(0)=1 gives x(t)=1−t1​, which explodes at t=1.
  • Stiffness: Euler on x˙=−10x multiplies x by 1−10h at each step: by −1.5 for h=0.25 (divergence), −0.5 for h=0.15. It is stable only for h<0.2.
Pitfalls
  • Without the Lipschitz condition, uniqueness fails and the flow map is not defined; without growth control, solutions can blow up in finite time.
  • Explicit Euler needs small steps on stiff problems (h<2/λ for x˙=−λx).
  • For a time-dependent field, vt​ must be evaluated at the current time: the trajectory of vt​ is not a trajectory of any frozen vs​.
In machine learning — neural ODEs and flow matching

A residual network xk+1​=xk​+fθ​(xk​) is Euler’s scheme for an ODE; neural ODEs take this literally. Flow matching (Lesson 6, OT4ML §16.1) learns a field vθ​(t,x) by regression, then generates a sample by drawing x0​∼N(0,I) and integrating x˙=vθ​(t,x) from t=0 to 1 with a few Euler or Runge–Kutta steps. Straighter trajectories, as produced by optimal-transport couplings, need fewer steps.

The continuity equation#

Used in Lesson 3 (displacement interpolation), Lesson 6 (Benamou–Brenier formula, flow matching), Lesson 8 (gradient flows: ∂t​α+div(αv)=0 with v=−∇δαδF​).

Mass is conserved: the mass in a region changes only by what flows through its boundary, and the flow of mass per unit time is density × velocity. Written for a density, this is a PDE; it is the Eulerian description (watch a fixed region) of particles moving along v (the Lagrangian description, previous reminder).

In the course OT4ML §14.1, eq. (14.2)–(14.3), p. 328; Prop. 14.2, p. 329; Thm. 14.5, p. 330

If particles follow x˙=vt​(x) with flow map Tt​, then αt​=(Tt​)#​α0​ solves the continuity equation

∂t​αt​+div(αt​vt​)=0,i.e.∫01​∫(∂t​φ+⟨vt​,∇x​φ⟩)dαt​dt=0

for all smooth compactly supported test functions φ(t,x) (weak form, valid for discrete measures too). Benamou–Brenier: W22​(α0​,α1​)=inf∫01​∫∥vt​∥2dαt​dt over all solutions (αt​,vt​) joining α0​ to α1​.

Along a trajectory (smooth density): dtd​logρt​(x(t))=−divvt​(x(t)) — the density decreases where the flow spreads out.

Worked example — moving and spreading a Gaussian
  1. The optimal map from N(0,1) to N(4,4) is T(x)=4+2x (§9), so particles move as xt​=(1−t)x+t(4+2x)=4t+(1+t)x and αt​=N(4t,(1+t)2).Affine image of a Gaussian (§3).
  2. Velocity at the point y=xt​: x˙t​=4+x=4+1+ty−4t​=:vt​(y).Express the particle velocity in terms of its current position.
  3. ∂t​ρt​+∂y​(ρt​vt​)=0: checked numerically at (t,y)=(0.3,1.7), the residual is 2×10−10.Finite differences on the explicit Gaussian density.
  4. Kinetic energy: ∫vt2​dαt​=E[(4+X)2]=16+1=17 for every t, and W22​=(0−4)2+(1−2)2=17.This path attains the Benamou–Brenier minimum: it is the optimal one.

Dilation: v(x)=ax in 1D keeps Gaussians, N(0,1)↦N(0,e2at), and along a trajectory dtd​logρt​=−a=−divv (checked numerically for a=0.5).

From particles to the equation
  1. dtd​∫φdαt​=dtd​∫φ(Tt​(x))dα0​(x)=∫⟨∇φ(Tt​(x)),∂t​Tt​(x)⟩dα0​(x).
    Definition of the push-forward, then the chain rule.
  2. =∫⟨∇φ(Tt​(x)),vt​(Tt​(x))⟩dα0​(x)=∫⟨∇φ,vt​⟩dαt​.
    ∂t​Tt​(x)=vt​(Tt​(x)) (the particle follows the field), then the push-forward again.
  3. For a smooth density, ∫⟨∇φ,vt​⟩ρt​=−∫φdiv(ρt​vt​), so ∫φ(∂t​ρt​+div(ρt​vt​))=0 for every φ: ∂t​ρt​+div(ρt​vt​)=0.Integration by parts (previous reminders); a function orthogonal to all test functions is zero.
Pitfalls
  • The velocity is not determined by the curve (αt​): adding a field w with div(αt​w)=0 (a rotation, for an isotropic Gaussian) gives the same αt​ (OT4ML p. 329). Benamou–Brenier selects the one of least kinetic energy, which is a gradient (OT4ML Prop. 14.3, p. 330).
  • The equation conserves mass; creating or destroying mass needs a source term (unbalanced OT).
  • For Diracs only the weak form makes sense.
In machine learning — continuous normalizing flows

For a learned field vθ​, integrating the last formula along a trajectory gives the log-likelihood of a continuous normalizing flow: logρ1​(x1​)=logρ0​(x0​)−∫01​divvθ​(t,xt​)dt (the divergence is estimated with random projections, Hutchinson’s trick). Flow matching avoids this computation at training time: it regresses vθ​ on the velocities of prescribed paths, and the continuity equation guarantees that the learned flow transports the noise to the data (OT4ML Prop. 16.3, p. 408).

Particles of U[0,2] follow x˙=−x. What is the law at time t, and how does it agree with dtd​logρt​(xt​)=−divv?

Answer

The flow map is Tt​(x)=e−tx, so the law is U[0,2e−t], with density 2et​ (≈1.36 at t=1). Here divv=−1, so the density along each trajectory must grow like et: it does, from 21​ to 2et​. The mass is squeezed into a shorter interval.

5. Convexity and optimization#

Convex problems have no spurious local minima, convex functions are envelopes of their tangent lines (Legendre transform), constraints can be priced by multipliers (duality), linear programs are solved at vertices, gradient methods descend, and functionals of measures can be differentiated too.

Convex sets and functions, strict and strong convexity, subgradients#

Used in Lesson 1 (Brenier: optimal maps are gradients of convex functions; convex costs on the line), Lesson 2 (the set of couplings is convex), Lesson 3 (Jensen), Lesson 4 (convex potentials, c-concavity), Lesson 7 (strict convexity of the entropic problem: a unique plan), Lesson 8 (convexity along geodesics, exponential convergence).

A set is convex if it contains the segment between any two of its points. A function is convex if its graph lies below its chords — equivalently above its tangents. Then every local minimum is global, and “the gradient vanishes” is enough to certify a minimum.

Definitions (standard)
  • f:Rd→R∪{+∞} is convex if f((1−t)x+ty)≤(1−t)f(x)+tf(y) for t∈[0,1]; strictly convex if the inequality is strict for x=y, t∈(0,1).
  • μ-strongly convex: f−2μ​∥⋅∥2 is convex. L-smooth: ∇f is L-Lipschitz. For f∈C2: convex ⟺∇2f⪰0; μ-strongly convex ⟺∇2f⪰μI; L-smooth ⟺−LI⪯∇2f⪯LI.
  • Subgradients: ∂f(x)={s: f(y)≥f(x)+⟨s,y−x⟩ ∀y}, the slopes of the lines that touch the graph at x from below. For differentiable convex f, ∂f(x)={∇f(x)}.
What convexity buys (standard)
  1. First-order characterisation (differentiable f): f convex ⟺f(y)≥f(x)+⟨∇f(x),y−x⟩ for all x,y.
  2. Every local minimum is global, and x⋆ is a minimiser ⟺0∈∂f(x⋆).
  3. Strictly convex: at most one minimiser. Strongly convex (and lower semi-continuous): exactly one, and f(x)−f(x⋆)≥2μ​∥x−x⋆∥2.
  4. Gradients of convex functions are monotone: ⟨∇f(x)−∇f(y),x−y⟩≥0 (in 1D: f′ is non-decreasing).
  5. Sums with nonnegative weights, suprema of convex functions, and compositions with affine maps are convex.
Worked example
  • f(x)=∣x∣: ∂f(0)=[−1,1] (all the lines through the origin with slope in [−1,1] stay below the graph), ∂f(x)={sign(x)} otherwise; 0∈∂f(0) certifies the minimum.
  • f(x1​,x2​)=x12​+x1​x2​+x22​: ∇2f=(21​12​) with eigenvalues 1 and 3, so f is 1-strongly convex and 3-smooth.
  • x4: strictly convex, not strongly (f′′(0)=0). ex: strictly convex with no minimiser (infimum 0, not attained). max(x2,(x−2)2) is convex; min(x2,(x−2)2) is not (two minimisers 0 and 2, and the chord between them lies below the bump at 1).
Proof that a local minimum of a convex function is global

Let x⋆ be a local minimum and y any point. For small t>0, xt​=(1−t)x⋆+ty is close to x⋆, so f(x⋆)≤f(xt​)≤(1−t)f(x⋆)+tf(y). Subtract (1−t)f(x⋆) and divide by t>0: f(x⋆)≤f(y).

Pitfalls
  • Strictly convex is not strongly convex (x4); strict convexity gives uniqueness, not existence (ex).
  • Convexity along straight lines (“flat” convexity) is not convexity along Wasserstein geodesics (“displacement” convexity), which Lesson 8 uses: a functional of measures can have one without the other.
In machine learning — convex losses, non-convex models

Least squares, logistic regression and support vector machines minimise convex losses in their parameters: any local minimum found by gradient descent is global. Neural networks are not convex in their weights. But the output of a two-layer network is linear in the distribution of its neurons, so the loss is convex as a function of that distribution — the starting point of the mean-field analysis of training as a Wasserstein gradient flow (OT4ML §15.4, p. 386; Lesson 8).

The Legendre–Fenchel transform (convex conjugate)#

Used in Lesson 1 and Lesson 4 (Brenier: the quadratic c-transform is a Legendre transform; the inverse of ∇φ is ∇φ∗; proof of Brenier’s theorem), Lesson 4 (dual formula of f-divergences, GANs), Lesson 7 (log-sum-exp and entropy are conjugate: soft c-transforms).

A convex function is the upper envelope of the lines below it. So it can be described by its supporting lines: for each slope y, keep the highest line of slope y that stays below the graph. Its intercept is −f∗(y), and f∗ is the convex conjugate (Legendre–Fenchel transform).

In the course OT4ML Def. 5.11, p. 100; p. 101

For h:Rd→R∪{+∞}:  h∗(y)=supx∈Rd​(⟨x,y⟩−h(x)) and h∗∗=(h∗)∗. If h is proper with an affine minorant, the Fenchel–Moreau theorem identifies h∗∗ with the greatest lower semi-continuous convex function below h. For the cost c(x,y)=21​∥x−y∥2 and φ(x)=21​∥x∥2−f(x), the c-transform is fc(y)=21​∥y∥2−φ∗(y).

Properties (standard)
  • f∗ is always convex and lower semi-continuous (a supremum of affine functions of y), even if f is not.
  • Fenchel–Young: f(x)+f∗(y)≥⟨x,y⟩ for all x,y, with equality iff y∈∂f(x) — iff the line of slope y touches the graph at x.
  • For f convex and lower semi-continuous: f∗∗=f. For f smooth and strictly convex: ∇f∗=(∇f)−1.
f(x)f∗(y)remark
21​∥x∥221​∥y∥2the only self-conjugate function
21​x⊤Ax, A≻021​y⊤A−1y∇f∗=A−1=(∇f)−1
p1​∣x∣pq1​∣y∣q,  p1​+q1​=1Fenchel–Young = Young’s inequality
∣x∣0 on [−1,1], +∞ outsidea norm ↔ the indicator of the dual ball
exylogy−y (y>0), 0 at 0, +∞ for y<0exponential ↔ entropy
log∑i​exi​∑i​yi​logyi​ on the simplex, +∞ off itsoft-max ↔ negative entropy (Lesson 7)
Worked example — f(x)=ex
  • For y>0, the concave function x↦xy−ex is maximal where y=ex, at x⋆=logy: f∗(y)=ylogy−y. For y=2: x⋆≈0.693, f∗(2)=2log2−2≈−0.614, and the tangent ℓ(x)=2x+0.614 has intercept −f∗(2).
  • Fenchel–Young at (x,y)=(1,e): f(1)+f∗(e)=e=1⋅e, equality since e=f′(1). At (0,2): 1−0.614=0.386>0, strict since 2=f′(0).
  • y<0: xy−ex→+∞ as x→−∞, so f∗(y)=+∞ (no line of negative slope stays below ex). y=0: f∗(0)=supx​(−ex)=0, approached but not attained.
  • Non-convex: for the double well f(x)=(x2−1)2, f∗∗ is the convex envelope, 0 on [−1,1] and f outside; f(0)=1 but f∗∗(0)=0.

Interactive figure (needs JavaScript).

What to look at: choose a function and move the slope y. The green line is the highest line of slope y below the graph; the green dot is where it touches (x⋆, the maximiser in the definition of f∗), and its intercept (open dot) is −f∗(y). The bottom panel plots f∗, and the readout checks Fenchel–Young at the contact point. For ex, negative slopes give +∞; for ∣x∣, every slope in (−1,1) touches at the corner 0 — the subdifferential [−1,1] — and f∗ is 0 there; for the non-convex double well, the slope 0 touches the graph at two points, ±1, and the line bridges the bump; other slopes touch once, outside [−1,1]. Either way f∗ only sees the convex envelope f∗∗ (dashed).

Proofs of Fenchel–Young and of ∇f∗=(∇f)−1

Fenchel–Young. f∗(y)≥⟨x,y⟩−f(x) for every x, by definition of a supremum. Equality holds iff x attains the supremum, i.e. ⟨x′,y⟩−f(x′)≤⟨x,y⟩−f(x) for all x′, i.e. f(x′)≥f(x)+⟨y,x′−x⟩: y∈∂f(x).

Inverse gradients. For smooth strictly convex f, the supremum defining f∗(y) is attained at the unique x with ∇f(x)=y. By the envelope theorem (below), ∇f∗(y)=x=(∇f)−1(y). This is why the inverse of a Brenier map ∇φ is ∇φ∗.

Pitfalls
  • Sign conventions: f∗ uses a sup of ⟨x,y⟩−f; the c-transform of optimal transport uses an inf of c−f (§9). Track the signs when you switch.
  • Infinite values are part of the transform (∣x∣↦ indicator of [−1,1]): do not drop them.
  • For a non-convex f, f∗∗=f: the conjugate forgets everything that is not in the convex envelope.
In machine learning — critics as dual variables

Duality turns a divergence into a maximisation over test functions, which a network can approximate. For KL, whose generator φ(s)=slogs−s+1 has conjugate φ∗(u)=eu−1: KL(α∣β)=supf​∫fdα−∫(ef−1)dβ, attained at f=logdβdα​ (OT4ML Prop. 7.24, p. 133). On a=(0.5,0.3,0.2), b=(0.2,0.3,0.5) the optimal f gives 0.2749=KL(a∣b); f=(1,0,−1) gives the lower bound 0.2724. With f a network evaluated on samples, this is an f-GAN discriminator, or a neural estimator of KL and mutual information. The Wasserstein-GAN critic is the analogous dual variable for W1​ (§4).

Compute the conjugate of f(x)=2a​x2 (a>0) and check Fenchel–Young at x=1.

Answer

xy−2a​x2 is maximal at x=y/a, so f∗(y)=2ay2​. Then ∇f∗(y)=y/a is the inverse of ∇f(x)=ax. At x=1 the contact slope is y=f′(1)=a, and f(1)+f∗(a)=2a​+2a​=a=1⋅a: equality, as it should be at a contact point.

Lagrangian duality and KKT conditions#

Used in Lesson 2 and Lesson 4 (the dual of the transport LP: the potentials are the multipliers of the marginal constraints), Lesson 6 (Benamou–Brenier: the multiplier of the continuity equation gives v=∇φ), Lesson 7 (entropic OT: the KKT conditions give P=diag(u)Kdiag(v); the sheet uses the Lagrangian and the envelope theorem).

Replace hard constraints by prices: violating a constraint costs its multiplier times the violation. For each choice of prices, minimising the penalised objective gives a lower bound on the true minimum; the best lower bound is the dual problem. For convex problems the bound is tight, and the optimal prices certify optimality.

Lagrangian and dual (standard)

Primal problem: p⋆=minf(x) subject to gi​(x)≤0 and hj​(x)=0. Lagrangian, with λ≥0 and μ free:

L(x,λ,μ)=f(x)+i∑​λi​gi​(x)+j∑​μj​hj​(x),q(λ,μ)=xinf​L(x,λ,μ),d⋆=λ≥0,μsup​q(λ,μ).
Duality theorems (standard)
  • Weak duality: d⋆≤p⋆ always.
  • Strong duality d⋆=p⋆ for convex problems (f,gi​ convex, hj​ affine) as soon as some feasible point satisfies all the inequalities strictly (Slater); for linear programs, as soon as the primal is feasible with a finite value.
  • KKT conditions: stationarity ∇f+∑λi​∇gi​+∑μj​∇hj​=0; primal feasibility; λ≥0; complementary slackness λi​gi​(x)=0. For a convex differentiable problem that satisfies Slater’s condition, x is optimal iff there are multipliers satisfying KKT.
  • Envelope theorem: if V(θ)=minz​F(z,θ) with a unique smooth minimiser z⋆(θ), then V′(θ)=∂θ​F(z⋆(θ),θ) — no need to differentiate z⋆. In particular the multiplier of a constraint is, up to the sign convention, the derivative of the optimal value with respect to the level of that constraint (example 1 below).
Worked examples
  1. Equality constraint. minx12​+x22​ s.t. x1​+x2​=1. L=x12​+x22​+μ(1−x1​−x2​); stationarity gives x1​=x2​=μ/2, the constraint μ=1: x⋆=(21​,21​), p⋆=21​. Dual function q(μ)=μ−2μ2​, maximal at μ=1: d⋆=21​=p⋆. Sensitivity: with x1​+x2​=c, p⋆(c)=2c2​, whose derivative at c=1 is 1=μ.
  2. Active inequality. min(x−2)2 s.t. x≤1: KKT gives 2(x−2)+λ=0, λ(x−1)=0, λ≥0, hence x=1, λ=2>0 (the constraint is active and has a positive price).
  3. Gibbs distribution — the softmax. minp∈Σn​​⟨c,p⟩−εH(p) with H(p)=−∑i​pi​logpi​. The multiplier of ∑i​pi​=1 gives ci​+ε(logpi​+1)+μ=0, so pi​=e−ci​/ε/∑j​e−cj​/ε, and the optimal value is the soft-min −εlog∑i​e−ci​/ε. For c=(0,1,2), ε=1: p≈(0.665,0.245,0.090), value ≈−0.408; for ε=0.1 the value is ≈−4.5×10−6, close to mini​ci​=0.
  4. Envelope. V(θ)=minz​(z2−2θz)=−θ2 with z⋆=θ; V′(1)=−2=∂θ​(z2−2θz)∣z=z⋆​=−2z⋆.
Proof of weak duality

Let x be feasible and λ≥0. Then λi​gi​(x)≤0 and hj​(x)=0, so q(λ,μ)≤L(x,λ,μ)≤f(x). Take the infimum over feasible x and the supremum over (λ,μ): d⋆≤p⋆. Equality, with optimal x⋆ and (λ⋆,μ⋆), forces both inequalities to be equalities: x⋆ minimises L(⋅,λ⋆,μ⋆) (stationarity) and ∑λi⋆​gi​(x⋆)=0 (complementary slackness).

Pitfalls
  • Multipliers of inequality constraints g≤0 must be ≥0 (with the convention +λg); multipliers of equalities have no sign.
  • Without convexity there can be a duality gap d⋆<p⋆.
  • In entropic OT the constraint P≥0 needs no multiplier: the entropy keeps the solution positive automatically.
In machine learning — softmax and attention are Lagrangian solutions

Example 3 says that softmax(s/ε) is the distribution that maximises ⟨s,p⟩+εH(p) over the simplex: an entropy-regularised argmax. Attention weights in transformers are such Gibbs distributions over keys, and Sinkhorn’s algorithm (Lesson 7) alternates two such normalisations so that both marginals of a plan are matched. Duality also explains support vector machines: only training points with a positive multiplier (the support vectors) enter the solution — complementary slackness.

Linear programming: polytopes, vertices, duality, complementary slackness#

Used in Lesson 2 (discrete Kantorovich is a linear program; sparse optimal plans), Lesson 3 (barycenters on a fixed grid), Lesson 4 (the dual LP, potentials, complementary slackness).

A linear program minimises a linear function over a polytope (a set cut out by finitely many linear inequalities). The level sets of a linear function are parallel hyperplanes: sliding them until they last touch the polytope, the contact happens at a vertex — or along a whole face.

In the course OT4ML Prop. 3.16, p. 57; Remark 3.19, p. 58; Prop. 5.2–5.3, p. 95
  • A linear form on a non-empty compact convex set has a minimiser that is an extreme point.
  • For general histograms one can choose an optimal plan whose support has no cycle, hence at most n+m−1 nonzero entries.
  • Discrete Kantorovich duality: Lc​(a,b)=P∈U(a,b)min​⟨C,P⟩=fi​+gj​≤Cij​max​⟨f,a⟩+⟨g,b⟩.
  • Complementary slackness: for P∈U(a,b) and admissible (f,g), ⟨C,P⟩−⟨f,a⟩−⟨g,b⟩=∑ij​Pij​(Cij​−fi​−gj​)≥0, and both are optimal iff Pij​>0⇒fi​+gj​=Cij​.
Worked example — the 2×2 transport problem of §1

a=(21​,21​), b=(41​,43​) on {0,1}, C=(01​10​) (cost ∣x−y∣). The couplings form the segment P(p), p∈[0,41​] (§1), and the cost 43​−2p is minimal at the vertex p=41​:

P⋆=(1/40​1/41/2​),⟨C,P⋆⟩=41​,3=n+m−1 nonzero entries.

Dual certificate. Complementary slackness on the support: f1​+g1​=0, f1​+g2​=1, f2​+g2​=0. Choosing f1​=0 gives g=(0,1), f=(0,−1). The last constraint holds: f2​+g1​=−1≤C21​=1. Dual value ⟨f,a⟩+⟨g,b⟩=−21​+43​=41​: equal to the primal value, so both are optimal. POT’s exact solver ot.emd returns the same plan and the potentials (0.625,−0.375), (−0.625,0.375): the same up to the shift (f+t,g−t). On random 6×5 problems it returns plans with exactly 10=n+m−1 nonzero entries.

Proof of weak duality and of complementary slackness

Use the marginal constraints: ⟨f,a⟩+⟨g,b⟩=∑i​fi​∑j​Pij​+∑j​gj​∑i​Pij​=∑ij​Pij​(fi​+gj​). Hence the gap ⟨C,P⟩−⟨f,a⟩−⟨g,b⟩=∑ij​Pij​(Cij​−fi​−gj​) is a sum of nonnegative terms (P≥0, fi​+gj​≤Cij​). It is zero iff every term is zero, i.e. iff P only charges the entries where the constraint is tight. A zero gap proves optimality of both: no plan costs less than a dual value, no dual value exceeds a plan’s cost.

Pitfalls
  • The optimum can be a whole face (non-unique solutions; e.g. ∣x−y∣ on the line, §2). Solvers return a vertex.
  • Dual potentials are never unique: (f+t1,g−t1) has the same value.
  • Size: n×m unknowns. Exact network-simplex solvers cost roughly O(n3logn) for n=m, which is what motivates entropic regularization (Lesson 7).
In machine learning — earth mover’s distances

Comparing two histograms with a ground cost by this LP is the “earth mover’s distance” of image retrieval; comparing two documents seen as weighted clouds of word embeddings is the word mover’s distance (OT4ML Example 4.11, p. 78). In Python, ot.emd(a, b, M) from the POT library solves the LP exactly and returns a sparse plan.

Gradient descent and stochastic gradient descent#

Used in Lesson 3 (the barycenter fixed-point algorithm is a descent method), Lesson 4 (semi-discrete OT by stochastic gradient ascent on the dual, OT4ML Prop. 6.9–6.10, p. 111–113), Lesson 6 (training flow matching), Lesson 7 (gradients of Sinkhorn losses), Lesson 8 (gradient flows; JKO = implicit Euler).

Walk downhill by small steps: xk+1​=xk​−τ∇f(xk​). With small steps you follow the gradient flow x˙=−∇f(x) (§4); with a noisy but unbiased estimate of the gradient you get stochastic gradient descent.

Convergence (standard)
  • Descent lemma. If f is L-smooth and τ≤1/L: f(xk+1​)≤f(xk​)−2τ​∥∇f(xk​)∥2.
  • Convex and L-smooth, τ≤1/L: f(xk​)−f⋆≤2τk∥x0​−x⋆∥2​. μ-strongly convex, τ=1/L: ∥xk​−x⋆∥2≤(1−Lμ​)k∥x0​−x⋆∥2 — linear convergence, slow when the condition number L/μ is large.
  • Quadratics f=21​x⊤Hx: each eigen-direction is multiplied by 1−τλi​ per step; convergence iff 0<τ<2/λmax​.
  • SGD: xk+1​=xk​−τk​gk​ with E[gk​∣xk​]=∇f(xk​). With steps ∑τk​=∞, ∑τk2​<∞ (Robbins–Monro) it converges for convex problems with bounded noise; with a constant step it oscillates in a region whose size grows with τ and the noise.
  • Implicit Euler (proximal point): xk+1​=argminx​f(x)+2τ1​∥x−xk​∥2. The JKO scheme of Lesson 8 is this step with ∥⋅∥2 replaced by W22​ (OT4ML Def. 15.1, p. 356).
Worked example
  • f(x)=21​(x12​+10x22​): L=10, μ=1. With τ=0.1: x2​ is multiplied by 0 (killed in one step) and x1​ by 0.9; after 10 steps x=(0.349,0). With τ=0.19: factors 0.81 and −0.9 (zigzag); after 10 steps (0.122,0.349). With τ=0.21: the factor −1.1 on x2​ makes it diverge (2.59 after 10 steps).
  • SGD computing a mean: minimise f(x)=21​E(x−Y)2 with the stochastic gradient xk​−yk​ and steps τk​=k+11​. Then xk+1​=xk​−k+1xk​−yk​​ is exactly the running average: on the samples 2,4,3,7 the iterates are 2,3,3,4 whatever x0​.
Proof of the descent lemma

L-smoothness gives the quadratic upper bound f(y)≤f(x)+⟨∇f(x),y−x⟩+2L​∥y−x∥2 (integrate ∇f along the segment and use the Lipschitz bound). With y=x−τ∇f(x): f(y)≤f(x)−τ(1−2Lτ​)∥∇f(x)∥2≤f(x)−2τ​∥∇f(x)∥2 when τ≤1/L.

Pitfalls
  • Too large a step diverges (τ>2/L on quadratics); ill-conditioning (L/μ large) makes small steps very slow.
  • On non-convex problems gradient descent finds stationary points, not necessarily global minima.
In machine learning — training is SGD, and SGD on neurons is a transport

Networks are trained by SGD and its variants (momentum, Adam) on minibatch losses; learning-rate decay schedules play the role of the Robbins–Monro conditions. For a wide two-layer network, gradient descent moves each neuron’s parameters as a particle; in the limit of infinitely many neurons, their distribution follows a Wasserstein gradient flow (OT4ML §15.4, p. 386; Lesson 8).

Derivatives of functionals of measures: the first variation#

Used in Lesson 8 (Wasserstein gradient flows and the JKO scheme; the exercise sheet computes first variations of φ-divergences, Dirichlet energies and interaction energies), Lesson 3 (optimality of barycenters), Lesson 7 (gradients of OT losses are dual potentials).

How does F(α) change when α changes a little? There are two ways to perturb a measure. Vertically: re-weight the mass, α→(1−ε)α+εβ; the derivative is a function of x, the first variation δαδF​. Horizontally: move the mass, α→(Id+εv)#​α; the derivative involves the spatial gradient ∇δαδF​, the Wasserstein gradient.

In the course OT4ML Def. 15.2, p. 356; Def. 15.5 and Prop. 15.7, p. 358

A function δαδF​(α) is the first variation of F at α if, for αε​=(1−ε)α+εβ,

F(αε​)=F(α)+ε∫δαδF​(α)d(β−α)+o(ε).

It is defined up to an additive constant (β−α has zero mass). The Wasserstein gradient is ∇x​δαδF​(α), and dτd​F((Id+τv)#​α)​τ=0​=∫⟨∇δαδF​,v⟩dα. The gradient flow is ∂t​αt​−div(αt​∇δαδF​(αt​))=0.

F(α)δαδF​(α)(x)gradient flow
potential energy ∫VdαV(x)each particle follows −∇V
interaction ∬W(x,y)dα(x)dα(y)∫(W(x,y)+W(y,x))dα(y) (=2∫W(x,y)dα(y) if W is symmetric)particles attract or repel each other
entropy ∫ρlogρdxlogρ(x)+1heat equation (OT4ML Ex. 15.13, p. 361)
KL(α∣β)logdβdα​(x) (+ const)Fokker–Planck (§8)
