Dirichlet energy 21​∫∥∇ρ∥2−Δρ (it is −2Δρ without the 21​, as in the Lesson 8 sheet)OT4ML Remark 15.14, p. 361
Worked example — vertical and horizontal derivatives of an interaction energy

α=21​δ0​+21​δ2​ and F(α)=∬∣x−y∣2dαdα, so F(α)=2⋅41​⋅4=2 and δαδF​(x)=2∫∣x−y∣2dα(y)=x2+(x−2)2.

  • Vertical, towards β=δ1​: the formula predicts F(αε​)−F(α)≈ε(δαδF​(1)−∫δαδF​dα)=ε(2−4)=−2ε. Direct computation: F(αε​)=2(1−ε), exactly.
  • Horizontal, moving the two atoms towards each other (v(0)=1, v(2)=−1): F=2(1−ε)2, derivative −4 at ε=0. Formula: ∇δαδF​(x)=4x−4, so ∫⟨∇δαδF​,v⟩dα=21​(−4)(1)+21​(4)(−1)=−4.
  • Non-symmetric kernel W(x,y)=xy2: F(α)=E[X]E[X2] and δαδF​(x)=xE[X2]+E[X]x2; the derivative towards δ1​ is −1, both by the formula and numerically.
From the vertical to the horizontal derivative

Moving the mass by Id+τv changes the measure, to first order, by −τdiv(αv) (the continuity equation, §4). Plug this zero-mass perturbation into the first variation and integrate by parts:

F((Id+τv)#​α)=F(α)−τ∫δαδF​div(αv)+o(τ)=F(α)+τ∫⟨∇δαδF​,v⟩dα+o(τ).

The steepest descent direction for the metric ∫∥v∥2dα is v=−∇δαδF​, which gives the gradient flow (OT4ML Prop. 15.7, p. 358).

Pitfalls
  • The first variation is defined only up to a constant: never compare two of them pointwise without fixing it.
  • Vertical and horizontal derivatives are different objects: for ∫Vdα the first is V, the second ∇V.
  • For particles α=n1​∑i​δxi​​, the ordinary gradient of F with respect to xi​ is n1​∇δαδF​(xi​): the Wasserstein gradient flow moves each particle with velocity −n∇xi​​F (OT4ML eq. (15.5), p. 360).
In machine learning — gradients of losses between distributions

To train a model with a loss between distributions, you need its derivative with respect to the model’s samples or weights. The table gives it: for an MMD loss, each generated sample moves along −∇x​∫k(x,y)d(α−β)(y); for an OT loss, the derivative with respect to the weights of α is a dual potential, which Sinkhorn computes for free (Lesson 7).

6. Information theory#

Entropy measures spread, the Kullback–Leibler divergence measures how badly one law explains another; both compare densities point by point, which makes them blind to geometry — the opposite of optimal transport — and exactly what entropic regularization adds to it.

Entropy and the Kullback–Leibler divergence#

Used in Lesson 4 (variational inference and the comparison of KL with W2​), Lesson 6 (Schrödinger bridges), Lesson 7 (entropic OT: H(P), KL(P∣a⊗b), mutual information; Sinkhorn = KL projections), Lesson 8 (entropy and KL as energies of gradient flows).

The entropy of a histogram measures how spread out it is: 0 for a Dirac, logn for the uniform law on n points. The Kullback–Leibler divergence KL(α∣β) is the average log-ratio logdβdα​ under α: how surprised you are, on average, when data from α are explained by the model β.

In the course OT4ML Def. 8.1, p. 136; Def. 8.7 and Prop. 8.8, p. 142; Def. 8.11 and Def. 8.13, p. 145
  • Entropy of a nonnegative matrix (or vector): H(P)=−∑ij​Pij​logPij​, with 0log0=0.
  • Relative entropy (generalized KL): KL(P∣Q)=∑ij​Pij​logQij​Pij​​−Pij​+Qij​, and +∞ if some Qij​=0<Pij​. For two probability vectors it reduces to ∑ij​Pij​logQij​Pij​​. Always KL(P∣Q)≥0, with equality iff P=Q.
  • For measures: KL(π∣ξ)=∫logdξdπ​dπ+ξ(X)−π(X) if π≪ξ, +∞ otherwise.
  • Mutual information of (X,Y)∼π with marginals α,β: I(X,Y)=KL(π∣α⊗β)≥0, zero iff X and Y are independent.
Useful facts (standard)
  • 0≤H(a)≤logn on Σn​, maximal for the uniform law. In bits, use log2​ (1 bit =log2 nats).
  • Cross-entropy: −∑i​ai​logbi​=H(a)+KL(a∣b).
  • Gaussians: KL(N(m1​,Σ1​)∣N(m2​,Σ2​))=21​[tr(Σ2−1​Σ1​)+(m2​−m1​)⊤Σ2−1​(m2​−m1​)−d+logdetΣ1​detΣ2​​]; differential entropy −∫ρlogρ=21​log((2πe)ddetΣ).
Worked example
  • a=(21​,41​,41​): H(a)=23​log2≈1.040 nats =1.5 bits; uniform b=(31​,31​,31​): H(b)=log3≈1.099.
  • KL(a∣b)=log3−H(a)≈0.0589 but KL(b∣a)≈0.0566: not symmetric.
  • a′=(21​,21​,0): KL(a′∣b)=log23​≈0.405 is finite, KL(b∣a′)=+∞ (b charges a point where a′ has no mass).
  • VAE term: KL(N(μ,σ2)∣N(0,1))=21​(σ2+μ2−1−logσ2); for μ=1, σ=0.5: ≈0.818 (numerical integration agrees).
  • The glued plan (3/81/8​1/83/8​) of Lesson 3 has mutual information ≈0.131 nats: its two coordinates are dependent, but far from deterministic (log2≈0.693 would be).
Proof that KL≥0 (Gibbs’ inequality)

For probability vectors with a≪b, Jensen with the convex function −log and the weights ai​:

KL(a∣b)=i∑​ai​(−logai​bi​​) ≥ −logi∑​ai​ai​bi​​=−logi:ai​>0∑​bi​ ≥ −log1=0.

Equality in Jensen for the strictly convex −log forces bi​/ai​ to be constant on the support of a, and the last inequality forces b to have no mass outside it: a=b. (The book’s proof uses φ(s)=slogs−s+1≥0 instead.)

Pitfalls
  • KL is not symmetric and not a distance.
  • KL(α∣β)=+∞ as soon as α charges a set that β does not. In particular the KL divergence between an empirical measure and a density is +∞: it cannot compare samples with a model directly.
  • Differential entropy can be negative (N(0,0.01): ≈−0.884) and changes under a change of coordinates; the discrete entropy cannot.
  • The book uses the generalized KL with the mass terms −P+Q, which matters for unnormalized measures (unbalanced OT) and vanishes for probabilities.
In machine learning — maximum likelihood is forward KL, variational inference is reverse KL

Maximum likelihood: Ex∼pdata​​[−logpθ​(x)]=H(pdata​)+KL(pdata​∣pθ​), so maximising the expected log-likelihood (or minimising the cross-entropy loss of a classifier) minimises the forward KL. It is mass-covering: pθ​ is heavily penalised wherever it misses data. Variational inference (and the ELBO of VAEs, §4) minimises the reverse KL(q∣p(⋅∣x)), which is mode-seeking: q is penalised wherever it puts mass that p does not have. The figure shows the difference on a single Gaussian fitted to two modes.

Compute KL(Bern(21​)∣Bern(41​)) and KL(Bern(41​)∣Bern(21​)).

Answer

21​log1/41/2​+21​log3/41/2​=21​log34​≈0.144, and 41​log1/21/4​+43​log1/23/4​≈−0.173+0.304=0.131. Two different numbers: KL is not symmetric.

f-divergences: KL, total variation, Hellinger, χ2#

Used in Lesson 3 (total variation), Lesson 4 (GANs; comparison with Wasserstein distances), Lesson 7 (KL is both a φ-divergence and a Bregman divergence; marginal penalties of unbalanced OT), Lesson 8 (gradient flows of φ-divergences, Exercise 1 of the sheet).

All these divergences compare two laws point by point through the ratio of their densities s=dβdα​, penalised by a convex function φ with φ(1)=0. They do not look at distances between points.

In the course OT4ML Def. 7.16, p. 130; Prop. 7.18 and Ex. 7.19–7.20, p. 130–131; Thm. 7.21, p. 131

For an entropy function φ (convex and lower semi-continuous on [0,∞), +∞ on negative numbers), normalised by φ(1)=0, and the Lebesgue decomposition α=dβdα​β+α⊥ (α⊥ is the part of α that β does not see),

Dφ​(α∣β)=∫φ(dβdα​)dβ+φ∞′​α⊥(X),discrete:  Dφ​(a∣b)=i:bi​>0∑​bi​φ(bi​ai​​)+φ∞′​i:bi​=0∑​ai​,

with φ∞′​=lims→∞​φ(s)/s. For probability measures Dφ​≥0, with equality iff α=β when φ is strictly convex. KL: φ(s)=slogs−s+1. Total variation: φ(s)=∣s−1∣, giving ∥α−β∥TV​ (full variation, no factor 21​). Pinsker: ∥α−β∥TV2​≤2KL(α∣β).

Pearson χ2(s−1)2∫ρβ​(ρα​−ρβ​)2​[0,∞]
Jensen–Shannon21​(slogs−(s+1)log2s+1​)21​KL(α∣2α+β​)+21​KL(β∣2α+β​)[0,log2]

Other classical inequalities: H2≤∥α−β∥TV​≤2H (with H2 the squared Hellinger distance of the table), and KL≤log(1+χ2)≤χ2. Data processing: Dφ​(T#​α∣T#​β)≤Dφ​(α∣β) — merging or transforming states can only lose information.

Worked example — the histograms of Lesson 3

a=(0.5,0.3,0.2) and b=(0.2,0.3,0.5) (the total-variation example of Lesson 3):

  • ∥a−b∥TV​=0.6, KL(a∣b)≈0.275 (here KL(b∣a) is the same, only because b is a reversed), H2≈0.135, χ2(a∣b)=0.63, JS≈0.066.
  • Pinsker: 0.62=0.36≤2×0.275=0.55. Hellinger: 0.135≤0.6≤2×0.368=0.735. χ2: 0.275≤log1.63=0.489≤0.63.
  • Data processing: merging the last two states gives (0.5,0.5) and (0.2,0.8); KL drops to 0.223, TV stays 0.6.

Blind to geometry. For two Diracs δ0​ and δε​ with ε=0: ∥⋅∥TV​=2, H2=2, JS=log2 and KL=χ2=+∞, however small ε is — while Wp​(δ0​,δε​)=∣ε∣ (Lesson 3).

Why Dφ​≥0

Take probability vectors a,b and let m=∑i:bi​=0​ai​ be the mass of a where b vanishes.

  1. ∑i:bi​>0​bi​φ(bi​ai​​) ≥ φ(∑i:bi​>0​bi​bi​ai​​)=φ(1−m).Jensen with the weights bi​, which sum to 1, and the convex φ.
  2. φ(1)≤φ(1−m)+mφ∞′​.The slopes of a convex function increase up to φ∞′​, so on [1−m,1] it grows by at most mφ∞′​.
  3. Dφ​(a∣b) ≥ φ(1−m)+mφ∞′​ ≥ φ(1)=0.Add the two lines: the second term of Dφ​ is exactly mφ∞′​.

When a≪b (m=0) this is just Jensen. The book’s proof handles general measures with the perspective function bφ(a/b) (OT4ML Prop. 7.18, p. 130).

Pitfalls — conventions
  • Total variation is sometimes defined with a factor 21​ (values in [0,1]), and Hellinger too. This course uses the full variation ∥α−β∥TV​=∫∣ρα​−ρβ​∣, with values in [0,2] (Lesson 3, OT4ML Ex. 7.20); with the factor 21​, Pinsker reads 21​∥α−β∥TV​≤KL/2​.
  • Jensen–Shannon: the book calls JS the square root of the divergence of the table (a distance) and writes JS2 for the divergence itself (OT4ML p. 132). This page writes JS for the divergence, as the GAN literature does.
  • χ2(α∣β) has ρβ​ in the denominator: it is not symmetric. The book’s power family normalises the generators differently (OT4ML p. 132).
  • On a continuous space φ-divergences do not metrize weak convergence: Riemann sums never converge to the uniform law for any of them.
In machine learning — why GAN losses saturate

With an optimal discriminator, the original GAN objective equals 2JS(pdata​,pθ​)−log4. When generated and real images live on different low-dimensional sets (the usual situation early in training), JS=log2 whatever the distance between these sets: the loss is flat and its gradient carries no information. Wasserstein GANs replace JS by W1​, which decreases as the generated distribution moves towards the data (OT4ML §7.4, p. 134; Lesson 4).

Bregman divergences#

Used in Lesson 7 (Sinkhorn as alternating KL projections and its convergence; Bregman-regularized OT), Lesson 8 (mirror descent, gradient flows in other geometries).

Take a strictly convex function Φ and its tangent at y. The gap between Φ(x) and the tangent, measured at x, is the Bregman divergence BΦ​(x∣y): it is ≥0, zero only at x=y, and it adapts the notion of “distance” to the geometry of Φ.

In the course OT4ML Def. 9.1–9.2, p. 172; Remark 7.23, p. 132; Prop. 8.34, p. 163

For a strictly convex differentiable (Legendre) function Φ:  BΦ​(P∣Q)=Φ(P)−Φ(Q)−⟨∇Φ(Q),P−Q⟩. The quadratic Φ=21​∥⋅∥2 gives 21​∥P−Q∥2; the negative entropy Φ(P)=∑Pij​logPij​ gives KL(P∣Q) (generalized). The Bregman projection of Q on a convex set C is argminP∈C​BΦ​(P∣Q). Except for KL, Bregman divergences and φ-divergences are different families; KL is their common case (OT4ML Prop. 8.34, p. 163).

Properties (standard)
  • BΦ​(x∣y)≥0 with equality iff x=y; convex in x; in general not symmetric and no triangle inequality.
  • Three-point identity: BΦ​(x∣y)+BΦ​(y∣z)−BΦ​(x∣z)=⟨∇Φ(z)−∇Φ(y),x−y⟩. It gives a Pythagorean inequality for Bregman projections, the engine of the convergence proof of Sinkhorn’s algorithm.
  • Centroid: argminc​∑i​wi​BΦ​(xi​∣c)=∑i​wi​xi​ (weights summing to 1): the arithmetic mean, for every Φ.
  • Mirror descent: ∇Φ(xk+1​)=∇Φ(xk​)−τ∇f(xk​). With the entropy on the simplex: xk+1​∝xk​⊙e−τ∇f(xk​) (exponentiated gradient).
Worked example
  • Φ(x)=xlogx on (0,∞): BΦ​(2∣1)=2log2−1≈0.386 and BΦ​(1∣2)=1−log2≈0.307: not symmetric. These are the generalized KL values xlogyx​−x+y.
  • Burg entropy Φ(x)=−logx gives the Itakura–Saito divergence yx​−logyx​−1: B(2∣1)≈0.307, B(1∣2)≈0.193.
  • Exponentiated gradient from the uniform x=(31​,31​,31​) with ∇f=(1,0,−1) and τ=1: x∝(e−1,1,e), i.e. (0.090,0.245,0.665) — the softmax of −∇f.
  • Centroid: for seven random positive vectors, the minimiser of ∑i​KL(xi​∣c) (generalized KL), found numerically, coincides with their arithmetic mean to six digits.
Proof of the centroid property

Let xˉ=∑i​wi​xi​. Expanding the definition,

i∑​wi​BΦ​(xi​∣c)−i∑​wi​BΦ​(xi​∣xˉ)=Φ(xˉ)−Φ(c)−⟨∇Φ(c),xˉ−c⟩=BΦ​(xˉ∣c)≥0,

because the terms Φ(xi​) cancel and ∑i​wi​(xi​−xˉ)=0. Equality iff c=xˉ.

Pitfalls
  • The order of the arguments matters: the centroid in the second argument is the arithmetic mean; in the first argument it is a “mirror” mean (for the generalized KL, the weighted geometric mean ∏i​xiwi​​).
  • Bregman divergences are not φ-divergences (except KL), and not distances.
In machine learning — mirror descent, clustering, Sinkhorn

Exponentiated-gradient (multiplicative-weights) updates are mirror descent with the entropy: they keep iterates on the simplex without projections and are standard in online learning and boosting. Because the best centroid is the mean for every Bregman divergence, k-means works unchanged with KL (e.g. to cluster word-count histograms). And Sinkhorn’s algorithm alternates KL projections on the row-sum and column-sum constraints (OT4ML Prop. 9.5, p. 175; Lesson 7).

7. Kernels#

A positive definite kernel is an inner product between feature vectors; averaging the features of a distribution embeds it in a Hilbert space, and the distance between two embeddings — the MMD — is a cheap, sample-friendly discrepancy that complements optimal transport.

Positive definite kernels, MMD and the energy distance#

Used in Lesson 4 (integral probability metrics; MMD versus W1​ in GANs), Lesson 5 (energy distance and sliced distances), Lesson 7 (Sinkhorn divergences interpolate between OT and an MMD; sample complexity), Lesson 8 (MMD and interaction-energy gradient flows).

A kernel k(x,y) is a similarity between points. It is positive definite when all its Gram matrices are PSD; then k(x,y)=⟨Φ(x),Φ(y)⟩ for some feature map Φ into a Hilbert space H (the RKHS). Represent a distribution by its mean feature mα​=∫Φdα; the maximum mean discrepancy is the distance between two mean features.

In the course OT4ML Def. 7.7 and Ex. 7.8, p. 127; Def. 7.9 and Prop. 7.10–7.11, p. 128; eq. (7.5), p. 129
  • k is positive definite if ∑i,j​ri​rj​k(xi​,xj​)≥0 for all points x1​,…,xn​ and all r∈Rn; conditionally positive definite if this holds for ∑i​ri​=0.
  • MMDk​(α,β)=∥α−β∥k​ with ∥ξ∥k2​=∬kdξdξ. For discrete measures:
    MMDk2​(α,β)=i,i′∑​ai​ai′​k(xi​,xi′​)+j,j′∑​bj​bj′​k(yj​,yj′​)−2i,j∑​ai​bj​k(xi​,yj​).
  • Dual form: MMDk​(α,β)=sup∥h∥H​≤1​∫hd(α−β). For a continuous kernel whose RKHS is dense in C(X) (universal kernel) on a compact X, MMDk​(αn​,α)→0⟺αn​⇀α.
  • Energy distance: the conditionally positive kernel −∥x−y∥ gives ED2(α,β)=2E∥X−Y∥−E∥X−X′∥−E∥Y−Y′∥ (X,X′∼α, Y,Y′∼β independent).
kernel k(x,y)what MMDk​ sees
linear ⟨x,y⟩only the means: MMD=∥mα​−mβ​∥
polynomial (1+⟨x,y⟩)pthe moments up to order p (not a distance between laws)
Gaussian e−∥x−y∥2/(2σ2), Laplace e−∥x−y∥/σeverything (characteristic kernels): MMD=0⟺α=β; scale set by σ
energy −∥x−y∥everything, with no scale parameter; in 1D ED2=2∫(Cα​−Cβ​)2
Worked example — α=21​δ0​+21​δ2​ against β=δ1​
  • Same mean (1): the linear kernel gives MMD=0, it cannot tell them apart.
  • Gaussian kernel, σ=1: Ek(X,X′)=21​⋅1+21​e−2 (same atom with probability 21​, distance 2 otherwise), Ek(Y,Y′)=1, Ek(X,Y)=e−1/2. So MMD2=0.568+1−1.213≈0.355, MMD≈0.595.
  • Bandwidth: σ=0.1 gives MMD2≈1.5 (points look all far apart), σ=10 gives ≈7×10−5 (the kernel is almost quadratic at this scale and nearly sees the means only).
  • Energy distance: E∣X−Y∣=1, E∣X−X′∣=21​⋅2=1, E∣Y−Y′∣=0, so ED2=2−1−0=1. With CDFs: Cα​−Cβ​=21​ on [0,1) and −21​ on [1,2), and 2∫(Cα​−Cβ​)2=2⋅21​=1. (And W1​=1.)
  • Gram matrix of the Gaussian kernel at the points 0,1,2: eigenvalues 0.21, 0.86, 1.93, all positive, as positive definiteness requires.
Why the MMD formula and the dual form agree

With k(x,y)=⟨Φ(x),Φ(y)⟩H​ and mα​=∫Φdα: ∥mα​−mβ​∥2=⟨mα​,mα​⟩−2⟨mα​,mβ​⟩+⟨mβ​,mβ​⟩=Ek(X,X′)−2Ek(X,Y)+Ek(Y,Y′), the formula above. For the dual form, the reproducing property h(x)=⟨h,Φ(x)⟩ gives ∫hd(α−β)=⟨h,mα​−mβ​⟩≤∥h∥∥mα​−mβ​∥ (Cauchy–Schwarz), with equality for h proportional to mα​−mβ​ (OT4ML Prop. 7.10, p. 128).

Pitfalls
  • The bandwidth matters: too small and every pair of distinct samples looks maximally different, too large and only low moments are compared.
  • Gaussian MMD saturates with distance: for two Diracs at distance d (σ=1), MMD2=2−2e−d2/2 is 0.79 for d=1, 1.98 for d=3, 2.00 for d=10 — far away, it no longer sees how far. The energy distance ED2=2d keeps growing, like transport distances.
  • The plug-in estimator with all pairs (including i=i′) is biased; the unbiased U-statistic drops the diagonal terms.
  • “Positive definite kernel” means PSD Gram matrices, not strictly positive ones.
In machine learning — two-sample tests, kernel GAN losses, KID

Given samples from two distributions, the empirical MMD is a test statistic for “same distribution?”, calibrated by permuting the labels of the pooled samples (kernel two-sample test). As a training loss, MMD gives MMD-GANs and generative moment matching networks; as an evaluation metric, the Kernel Inception Distance is an MMD with a polynomial kernel on network features (OT4ML Example 7.14, p. 129). Its main advantage over OT is statistical: the empirical MMD converges at the rate n−1/2 in any dimension (OT4ML Prop. 10.11, p. 203), whereas Wp​ suffers from the curse of dimensionality (§1). Sinkhorn divergences interpolate between the two: OT when ε→0, half the squared MMD with kernel −c when ε→∞ (OT4ML Prop. 8.40, p. 168; Lesson 7).

With the linear kernel k(x,y)=xy on R, show that MMDk​(α,β)=∣mα​−mβ​∣, the difference of the means.

Answer

For independent X,X′∼α and Y,Y′∼β: E[XX′]=mα2​, E[YY′]=mβ2​, E[XY]=mα​mβ​. So MMD2=mα2​+mβ2​−2mα​mβ​=(mα​−mβ​)2. Two laws with the same mean are at MMD 0 for this kernel: it is not characteristic.

8. Stochastic processes#

Brownian motion is the continuous random walk; adding it to an ODE gives a stochastic differential equation, whose law evolves by the Fokker–Planck equation — a continuity equation whose velocity contains the score ∇logρ. Only what the course needs is recalled here.

Brownian motion and stochastic differential equations#

Used in Lesson 6 (stochastic interpolants, Schrödinger bridges, diffusion models), Lesson 7 (entropic OT is a static Schrödinger problem; its Gibbs kernel is a Gaussian heat kernel), Lesson 8 (Langevin dynamics, diffusion models, noisy particle systems).

A Brownian motion is the limit of a random walk with many tiny independent steps. Its displacement over a time t is Gaussian with variance t: it spreads like t​, not like t. A stochastic differential equation adds such noise to an ODE: a deterministic drift plus random kicks.

Definitions and rules (standard, informal)
  • Brownian motion (Bt​)t≥0​ in Rd: B0​=0, continuous paths, independent increments, Bt​−Bs​∼N(0,(t−s)I). Its paths are nowhere differentiable: “dBt​/dt” does not exist.
  • SDE dXt​=b(Xt​)dt+σdBt​, made rigorous as an Itô integral equation and simulated by Euler–Maruyama: Xk+1​=Xk​+hb(Xk​)+σh​ξk​, ξk​∼N(0,I) independent.
  • Itô’s formula (1D): df(Xt​)=f′(Xt​)dXt​+21​σ2f′′(Xt​)dt. The extra second-order term comes from (dBt​)2=dt. Taking expectations: dtd​Ef(Xt​)=E[b(Xt​)f′(Xt​)+2σ2​f′′(Xt​)].
  • Langevin dynamics dXt​=−∇V(Xt​)dt+2​dBt​: its law converges (under mild conditions) to the density ∝e−V.
Worked example
  • P(∣B1​∣≤1)≈0.683 and P(∣B1​∣≤2)≈0.954: the envelopes of the figure.
  • Itô with f(x)=x2 and X=B (b=0, σ=1): d(Bt2​)=2Bt​dBt​+dt, so EBt2​=t. The ordinary chain rule would miss the dt.
  • Euler–Maruyama for dX=−Xdt+2​dB (an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process, stationary law N(0,1)): Xk+1​=(1−h)Xk​+2h​ξk​. Its stationary variance v solves v=(1−h)2v+2h, so v=2−h2​: 1.053 for h=0.1 (six simulations with 200000 chains each give values within 0.005 of it), 1.005 for h=0.01. The discretisation bias vanishes like h.
Where the 21​σ2f′′ comes from

Over a small time step h, ΔX≈bh+σΔB with ΔB∼N(0,h). Taylor: f(X+ΔX)−f(X)≈f′(X)ΔX+21​f′′(X)(ΔX)2. Now (ΔX)2≈σ2(ΔB)2 has mean σ2h — the same order as the drift term, not smaller — while its fluctuations are of order h times a centred variable and average out over many steps. Summing over steps gives ∫21​σ2f′′dt. For a smooth path, (ΔX)2=O(h2) and the term disappears: this is the difference between stochastic and ordinary calculus.

Pitfalls
  • Noise scales like h​, drift like h: in Euler–Maruyama the noise term is σh​ξ, not σhξ.
  • Conventions for the noise level differ: 2​dB (this page), σdB, or 2σ​dB. With noise 2​sdB the Laplacian term of Fokker–Planck is s2Δ (OT4ML p. 363 writes it this way). Check before reusing a formula.
  • Itô calculus is not ordinary calculus (previous example); another convention (Stratonovich) keeps the ordinary chain rule but changes the drift.
In machine learning — Langevin sampling and diffusion models

The unadjusted Langevin algorithm xk+1​=xk​+h∇logp(xk​)+2h​ξk​ samples approximately from p using only its score ∇logp (no normalising constant). Score-based diffusion models learn the score of noised data with a network and run a reverse-time SDE (or an ODE with the same marginals, next) from noise to data (OT4ML §16.1, p. 407; Remark 16.5, p. 410). Small-step SGD is sometimes modelled by such an SDE, although its noise can be heavy-tailed (OT4ML Remark 15.60, p. 397).

The heat equation, Fokker–Planck and Ornstein–Uhlenbeck#

Used in Lesson 8 (Fokker–Planck is the Wasserstein gradient flow of a free energy; the heat equation that of the entropy; convergence rates), Lesson 6 (probability-flow ODEs of diffusion models), Lesson 7 (heat kernels and Gibbs kernels).

Follow not one noisy particle but the density ρt​ of a whole cloud. The drift transports it (a continuity equation, §4), the noise spreads it (a Laplacian). The resulting PDE is the Fokker–Planck equation.

In the course OT4ML p. 363 and Example 15.15; Example 15.13, p. 361

If dXt​=b(Xt​)dt+2​sdBt​, the density of Xt​ solves  ∂t​ρt​=−div(bρt​)+s2Δρt​. For b=−∇V this is the W2​ gradient flow of the free energy ρ↦∫Vρdx+s2∫ρlogρdx. Without drift (V=0, s=1), the entropy flow is the heat equation ∂t​ρ=Δρ.

Three ways to read Fokker–Planck (s=1, standard)
  • As a continuity equation: ∂t​ρ+div(ρv)=0 with v=b−∇logρ (because Δρ=div(ρ∇logρ)). Particles moving with this deterministic velocity have the same laws ρt​ as the SDE.
  • As relaxation to equilibrium: for b=−∇V and ρ∞​∝e−V, ∂t​ρ=div(ρ∇logρ∞​ρ​), and KL(ρt​∣ρ∞​) decreases; under a logarithmic Sobolev inequality with constant λ it decays like e−2λt (OT4ML Prop. 15.42, p. 381).
  • Heat equation (b=0): ρt​=ρ0​∗N(0,2tI), convolution with a Gaussian of variance 2t.

Ornstein–Uhlenbeck (V(x)=21​∥x∥2): Xt​=e−tX0​+1−e−2t​Z with Z∼N(0,I) independent of X0​. Gaussians stay Gaussian: N(m,σ2)↦N(e−tm, e−2tσ2+1−e−2t)→N(0,1). Here λ=1.

Worked example — OU from N(3,0.25)
  • At t=1: mean 3e−1≈1.104, variance 0.25e−2+1−e−2≈0.898.
  • KL(ρt​∣N(0,1))=21​(v+m2−1−logv): 4.818 at t=0, 0.612 at t=1, 0.082 at t=2 — below the log-Sobolev bound 4.818e−2t, which gives 0.652 and 0.088.
  • The heat equation is checked by finite differences on ρt​=N(0,0.5+2t) at (t,x)=(0.4,0.7): ∂t​ρ=−0.13890=∂xx​ρ.
From Itô’s formula to Fokker–Planck
  1. dtd​∫fρt​=dtd​Ef(Xt​)=E[⟨b(Xt​),∇f(Xt​)⟩+Δf(Xt​)]=∫(⟨b,∇f⟩+Δf)ρt​.
    Itô’s formula in Rd with noise 2​dB: the second-order term is 21​⋅2Δf.
  2. =∫f(−div(bρt​)+Δρt​).
    Integrate by parts once in the first term, twice in the second (§4).
  3. This holds for every test function f, hence ∂t​ρt​=−div(bρt​)+Δρt​.Two densities with the same integrals against all test functions are equal.
Pitfalls
  • The factor in front of Δ depends on the noise convention (previous reminder).
  • The stationary density is ∝e−V for gradient drifts b=−∇V. For a general drift there is no such formula: the equilibrium solves div(bρ)=Δρ, which is rarely explicit.
  • The equation is linear in ρ, but its velocity b−∇logρ depends on ρ: the deterministic particle picture needs the score of the current density.
In machine learning — diffusion models run an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process backwards

The forward noising process of a variance-preserving diffusion model is an OU process: Xt​=e−tX0​+1−e−2t​Z turns any data distribution into nearly N(0,I). A network sθ​(t,x) is trained to approximate the score ∇logρt​ (denoising score matching). Generation integrates the reverse-time SDE, or the probability-flow ODE x˙=−x−∇logρt​(x) backwards from noise: it is the velocity b−∇logρ above, so its particles have the same marginals ρt​ (OT4ML Remark 16.5, p. 410–411).

Start the Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process dX=−Xdt+2​dB at the point X0​=3. What is the law of X1​, and its W2​ distance to N(0,1)?

Answer

X1​=3e−1+1−e−2​Z∼N(1.104,0.9302). By the 1D Gaussian formula (§9), W22​=1.1042+(0.930−1)2≈1.223, so W2​≈1.106: after one unit of time the Dirac has become a nearly standard Gaussian, only shifted.

9. The optimal transport facts every lesson reuses#

Five results are used everywhere: Monge’s problem and Brenier’s theorem, Kantorovich’s relaxation as a linear program, the Wasserstein distances, duality with c-transforms, and the closed forms on the line and for Gaussians. Here they are in one place, each with a check on numbers and a link to the lesson that proves it.

Monge’s problem and Brenier’s theorem#

Proved in Lesson 1 (statement, 1D and Gaussian cases) and Lesson 4 (proof through duality). Refresher in Lesson 3.

The facts OT4ML Def. 2.14, p. 25; Thm. 2.23, p. 29
  • Monge: T: T#​α=βmin​∫c(x,T(x))dα(x) — move each point to one destination. The constraint set can be empty: no map sends δ0​ to 21​δ−1​+21​δ1​ (a map cannot split a Dirac, §1).
  • Brenier: on Rd with c(x,y)=∥x−y∥2, if α has a density and both measures have finite second moments, there is a unique optimal map, and it is the gradient of a convex function: T=∇φ. The optimal plan is (Id,T)#​α.
  • In 1D, “gradient of a convex function” means “non-decreasing”: T=Cβ−1​∘Cα​ (§2). Between Gaussians, T is affine with a symmetric positive matrix (§3).
Check

α=N(0,1), β=N(2,9) on R: T(x)=2+3x=φ′(x) with φ(x)=23​x2+2x convex, and T#​α=N(2,9). Cost: E[(X−T(X))2]=E[(2+2X)2]=4+4=8=(0−2)2+(1−3)2.

Kantorovich’s problem: couplings and the linear program#

Proved in Lesson 2 (discrete case, linear programming, Birkhoff) and Lesson 3 (general measures).

The facts OT4ML Def. 3.31, p. 66; Prop. 3.34, p. 66; Cor. 3.18, p. 58
  • Lc​(α,β)=π∈U(α,β)min​∫cdπ=X∼α, Y∼βmin​E[c(X,Y)]: optimise over couplings (§1) — mass may be split. The set of couplings is never empty (α⊗β) and the minimum is attained for lower semi-continuous costs.
  • Discrete case: the linear program min{⟨C,P⟩: P≥0, P1=a, P⊤1=b} (§5); there is an optimal plan with at most n+m−1 nonzero entries; for n=m and uniform weights, an optimal permutation (§3), so Monge and Kantorovich agree.
  • When Brenier applies, the Kantorovich optimum is the Monge map: π=(Id,∇φ)#​α.
Check

δ0​ to 21​δ−1​+21​δ1​ with ∣x−y∣2: Monge is impossible, but the only coupling sends half of the mass to each point, at cost 21​+21​=1. The 2×2 example of §5 has optimal cost 41​ with the plan (1/40​1/41/2​).

Wasserstein distances#

Proved in Lesson 3 (distance, comparison, convergence, geodesics, barycenters); Lesson 4 (the dual formula of W1​).

The facts OT4ML Def. 4.6 and Prop. 4.7, p. 76; Prop. 4.17, p. 80; Prop. 4.25, p. 83
  • Wp​(α,β)=(minπ∈U(α,β)​∫d(x,y)pdπ)1/p, p≥1, is a distance on Pp​(X); the triangle inequality comes from gluing plans and Minkowski (§4).
  • Wp​(δx​,δy​)=d(x,y); Wp​≤Wq​ for p≤q; Wp​-convergence is weak convergence plus convergence of p-th moments (§1).
  • W2​ has constant-speed geodesics (displacement interpolation, a continuity equation, §4) and barycenters. W1​(α,β)=supLip(f)≤1​∫fd(α−β) (Kantorovich–Rubinstein, §4).
Check

Moving a mass ε by a distance 1: Wp​(δ0​,(1−ε)δ0​+εδ1​)=ε1/p, so W1​=ε but W2​=ε​ (Lesson 3). Versus total variation (§6): ∥δ0​−δε​∥TV​=2 while Wp​=ε.

Duality and c-transforms#

Proved in Lesson 4; the discrete version is LP duality (§5), used in Lesson 2; the entropic version is the subject of Lesson 7.

The facts OT4ML Prop. 5.5, p. 96; Def. 5.8 and Prop. 5.9, p. 99; Prop. 5.12, p. 101
  • Lc​(α,β)=f(x)+g(y)≤c(x,y)max​∫fdα+∫gdβ (compact spaces, continuous cost). The potentials f,g are prices; at the optimum f(x)+g(y)=c(x,y) wherever the optimal plan puts mass (complementary slackness).
  • c-transform: fc(y)=infx​(c(x,y)−f(x)) is the best g for a given f; it inherits the regularity of c (§4).
  • Quadratic cost 21​∥x−y∥2: with φ=21​∥⋅∥2−f, fc=21​∥⋅∥2−φ∗ — the Legendre transform (§5); this is how Brenier’s theorem is proved. For c=d: g=−f with f 1-Lipschitz, giving the W1​ formula.
Check

In the 2×2 example of §5, f=(0,−1) and g=(0,1): g is the c-transform of f, since mini​(Ci1​−fi​)=min(0,2)=0=g1​ and mini​(Ci2​−fi​)=min(1,1)=1=g2​. Dual value 41​, equal to the primal one.

Closed forms: the line and Gaussians#

Proved in Lesson 1; used in Lesson 3 (barycenters), Lesson 5 (sliced OT: the 1D formula on every projection), Lesson 7 (entropic Gaussians).

The facts OT4ML Prop. 2.44, p. 38–39; Prop. 2.56, p. 46
  • On the line, for p≥1: Wpp​(α,β)=∫01​​Cα−1​(t)−Cβ−1​(t)​pdt, and W1​(α,β)=∫R​∣Cα​(x)−Cβ​(x)∣dx (§2). For point clouds of equal size: sort and match (§2).
  • Gaussians: W22​(N(mα​,Σα​),N(mβ​,Σβ​))=∥mα​−mβ​∥2+B(Σα​,Σβ​)2 with the Bures term of §3; in 1D, (mα​−mβ​)2+(σα​−σβ​)2.
Check

U[0,1] and U[a,1+a]: the quantile functions are t and t+a, so Wp​=a for every p. W22​(N(0,I),N(0,S))=6−2(3​+1)≈0.536 for S=(21​12​) (§3). Point clouds (0,1,3) and (1,2,5): W22​=2 (§2).

Compute W2​(U[0,1],δ1/2​) with the quantile formula.

Answer

The quantile functions are t and the constant 21​, so W22​=∫01​(t−21​)2dt=121​ and W2​=23​1​≈0.289 — the standard deviation of the uniform law, as it must be: the only coupling with a Dirac sends everything to it.

Sources of this page#

  • The course resources: G. Peyré, Optimal Transport for Machine Learners (OT4ML.pdf; references “OT4ML” give the statement number and the PDF page), and its compact version (CourseOT-compact.pdf); G. Peyré and M. Cuturi, Computational Optimal Transport (1803.00567v4.pdf); S. Chewi, J. Niles-Weed and P. Rigollet, Statistical Optimal Transport (2407.18163v2.pdf); the exercise sheets of each lesson.
  • The facts marked “standard” are textbook material in probability (laws of large numbers, CLT, conditional expectation, Brownian motion), linear algebra (spectral theorem, matrix functions), analysis (inequalities, compactness, change of variables, ODEs, divergence theorem), convex optimization (convexity, conjugates, Lagrangian duality, linear programming, gradient methods) and information theory (entropy, divergences). For the optimal-transport side, F. Santambrogio, Optimal Transport for Applied Mathematicians, listed in the course bibliography, covers the same ground with full proofs.
  • Notes on conventions: total variation is the full variation, in [0,2] (OT4ML Ex. 7.20, §6); the book’s JS is the square root of the Jensen–Shannon divergence used on this page (OT4ML p. 132); the noise 2​sdBt​ gives the term s2Δρ in Fokker–Planck (OT4ML p. 363, §8); the book writes the Bures sandwich as Σ1/2ΛΣ1/2, the board of Lesson 3 in the other order, with the same trace (§3).
  • All the numbers of the worked examples were computed with Python (NumPy, SciPy and the POT library) before being written.
